entry.title: Lazer Updates Top-Tier Impala KinetiCore MTB Helmet with Adjustable Straps to Solve Comfort Issue
entry.content:
Last fall, Lazer debuted the new Impala KinetiCore mountain bike helmet. As the brand’s top-of-the-line half-shell lid, the Impala is packed with unique safety tech, including KinetiCore and DualCore, along with all the features we’ve come to expect in modern trail-riding helmets. Lazer sent me one to test pre-launch, and I liked nearly everything about it. Except for one glaring issue: a sewn, non-adjustable strap design that made it nearly unwearable for me.

It seems I wasn’t alone. Our Editor-in-Chief Zach Overholt didn’t get along with the Impala’s straps either. Nearly every other Impala review I read also mentioned this curious design choice causing discomfort and annoyance on an otherwise solid helmet. While the fixed-strap design may work for some helmets, it clearly was not the right choice for the Impala KinetiCore. It’s fair to assume the negative reviews and feedback probably resulted in low sales, too. 

Way back at Sea Otter last April, the Lazer folks told us they heard the criticism, took the feedback to heart, and would be updating the straps. Now, several months later, we just learned that Lazer has finally updated the Impala KinetiCore for 2027 with an adjustable ear cradle strap design. 

Problem Solved

I just received the updated Impala KinetiCore, and I’m happy to report that the discomfort issue has been completely resolved. Straight out of the box, the straps are aligned more comfortably, and it no longer forces the chin strap to rest against my throat. Even if it wasn’t perfect out of the box, the adjustable ear cradle allows you to reposition it to personalize the fit. A seriously simple fix to a serious comfort issue.

It’s unfortunate that Lazer didn’t use an adjustable ear cradle system to begin with, but I’m happy to see they listened to consumer and reviewer feedback and fixed this glaring issue moving forward. With the updated strap design, I can actually wear the Impala KinetiCore without feeling like the straps are trying to choke me. Now, I feel comfortable recommending this helmet to anyone, without needing to say, “if the position of the sewn straps works for you.”

Extended Satisfaction Guarantee

The folks at Lazer also recognize that some people who purchased the 2026 Impala KinetiCore may be dissatisfied with its comfort due to the fixed strap design. For those folks, Lazer is doubling its typical 60-day satisfaction guarantee. 

“Lazer is extending the satisfaction guarantee on MY26 Impala KinetiCore to 120 days in order to give consumers who have made a purchase in recent months an opportunity to switch to the MY27 Impala KinetiCore with the updated strap-slider-equipped product at no charge. Please contact your original point of purchase to make a qualified return.”

With the new adjustable straps, my initial complaints about discomfort are no longer valid. This is a well-rounded trail riding helmet that checks a lot of boxes and is certainly worthy of consideration. Check it out at Lazersport.com

entry.title: Firsthand Framebuilding School is Hiring
entry.content:
Firsthand Framebuilding, Portland’s new handlearning center for framebuilders, is hiring. If you are interested in joining its small team, they would love to hear from you and have the following positions open…

The Customer Experience & Fulfillment Coordinator is responsible for the day-to-day execution and organization of customer service, order fulfillment, shipping, receiving, inventory, and supply shop operations.

This role plays an important part in the entire customer experience. From helping customers identify and purchase the right products to ensuring their orders are fulfilled accurately and efficiently.

The ideal person for this role is highly organized, detail-oriented, comfortable working with systems, and enjoys helping customers. They should be equally comfortable answering a customer question, packing an order, receiving inventory, and working within Shopify and related systems.

Schedule: Full-time, 40 hours per week
Compensation: $55,000 annually
Benefits: Flexible PTO; tax-free healthcare stipend
Location: Portland, Oregon

The Program Manager is responsible for day-to-day execution of classes and the operational systems that support our educational programming.

This role ensures classes run smoothly, efficiently, and professionally while maintaining materials readiness, supporting instructors, managing purchasing and inventory for the classes.

This is a hands-on, detail-oriented role blending class execution, operational coordination, inventory management, and supply operations.

Schedule: 32 hours per week
Compensation: $60,000 annual salary
Benefits: Flexible PTO; tax-free healthcare stipend
Location: Portland, Oregon

See more at the Firsthand Framebuilding Careers Page.

entry.title: Velocio Adds New LUXE, ONE, and TRAIL Apparel for Fall and Winter Riding
entry.content:
Velocio makes some of the finest cycling apparel in the industry, and the brand is constantly updating existing models or adding new pieces to its various lineups. For fall/winter 2026, the brand recently introduced several new garments designed to be adaptable and help take the guesswork out of dressing for fall riding. 

For road and gravel riders, the LUXE collection grows with new vests, jackets, and accessories, along with the new ONE Thermal Bib Tights. On the mountain bike side, the brand-new TRAIL Merino Long Sleeve and Air Pullover offer more options for riding in cool temperatures while chasing the best conditions of the year.

“Nobody wants to stand in their kitchen every morning trying to solve a weather puzzle,” said Velocio design director and co-founder Brad Sheehan. “We designed this collection to simplify that moment. These pieces work together to perform across changing conditions so that you can start pedalling without overthinking or overpacking.”

LUXE Air Vest and Jacket

Velocio is adding to its popular LUXE line with the new Air Vest and Air Jacket. Both are designed to “deliver exceptional warmth in a lightweight build that wears more like a jersey than a winter jacket.” Of course, the jacket has full sleeves while the vest does not; otherwise, they feature the same materials and construction. 

With body-mapped active insulation and a protective shell up front, and jersey-weight fleece on the back, the LUXE Air Vest and Jacket aim to provide wind and weather protection with reliable, adaptable thermal regulation. Both have two-way zippers and come in men’s and women’s versions in Dark Slate and Dark Sulphur colorways.

  • Japanese-milled 55g, 100% recycled polyester front body fabric
  • Body-mapped 80g active insulation
  • Fleece back (and underarms on jacket) to improve breathability
  • Performance-focused on-bike fit reduces flapping-Two-way front zipper
  • Colors: Dark Slate, Dark Sulphur
  • Sizes: Men: XS – XXXXL, Women: XXS – XXXL
  • LUXE Air Vest MSRP: $229 
  • LUXE Air Jacket MSRP: $269

ONE Thermal Bib Tights

Velocio calls the new ONE Thermal Bib Tight “a versatile three-season workhorse with balanced compression for mid-distance rides and lightweight thermal insulation for everything from cool mornings to brisk winter days.” According to the brand, it slots in between the standard LUXE Bib Tight and the LUXE Thermal Bib Tight in terms of warmth and protection from the elements. It’s warmer than the former, but not as insulating, windproof, or compressive as the latter — striking a balance for riders who only want ONE bib tight for all their cool-cold weather riding.

The ONE Thermal Bib Tight is made from a recycled thermal fabric with a lightweight fleece lining and moderate compression for mid-distance rides. It features Velocio’s multi-density Signature Chamois, and the women’s version includes the FreeFly design to facilitate bathroom breaks without the need to remove layers.

  • Recycled thermal fabric and lightweight fleece lining
  • Moderate compression for mid-distance versatility
  • Full-length coverage for cool to cold weather riding
  • Signature chamois combines multi-density layers with refined edges and a perforated top
  • Designed in the on-bike position for pedaling without constriction
  • FlyFree design on Women’s for easy bathroom breaks
  • Color: Black
  • Sizes: Men: XS – XXXXL, Women: XXS – XXXL
  • MSRP: $199

TRAIL Merino Long Sleeve

The new TRAIL Merino Long Sleeve was designed to be an all-day essential for mountain biking once the temperatures drop. It features a grid-knit heavyweight merino blend fabric on the front and arms with a midweight mesh back for breathability. The denser front and arm fabric stands up to brushes with trailside obstacles and blocks a little wind, while the grid texture inside is claimed to “lift off your skin to trap warmth while creating channels that move air, wicking away sweat and excess heat.” 

The TRAIL Merino Long Sleeve comes in men’s and women’s versions in three colors: Black, Rocky Ridge (beige), and Deep Forest. We’ve got one in for testing and will follow up with a review in the near future.

  • Materials: 75% polyamide, 25% virgin wool
  • Heavyweight grid construction, front and arms
  • Midweight mesh back for breathability
  • Boxy fit looks casual without being so loose it snags
  • Colors: Black, Rock Ridge, and Deep Forest
  • Sizes: Men: XS – XXXXL, Women: XXS – XXXL
  • MSRP: $119

Air Pullover

The all-new Air Pullover is designed to be worn on its own or as a cold-weather layering piece, whether you’re on the bike or not. It features a featherlight 95g high-loft fleece covering the front, shoulders, and back, paired with merino grid sleeves. Velocio says the fleece body “traps heat when you’re taking it easy, and turbocharges breathability and wicking when you’re on the move.” Meanwhile, the merino-grid sleeves add durability and also aid with thermal regulation.

Velocio says that it’s a great piece to wear on its own while riding, to the trailhead, or kicking it around the house. When temperatures are frigid, layer it under a shell and/or add a base layer to crank up the warmth. Like all of the other Velocio pieces listed here, the Air Pullover comes in men’s and women’s versions. We’ve also got one of these in for testing and will follow up with a review once it’s cool enough to try it out.

  • Hybrid construction
  • High-loft lightweight fleece main body
  • Merino grid sleeves
  • Active insulation stretches, breathes, and thermoregulates
  • Easily worn as a layer or standalone piece
  • Relaxed, boxy, pullover cut
  • Colors: Red Ochre, Black
  • Sizes: Men: XS – XXXXL, Women: XXS – XXXL
  • MSRP: $189

Availability

All of Velocio’s new and updated fall/winter 2026 cycling apparel is available now. Head to the Velocio website to learn more, see the brand’s full lineup of cycling apparel, or pick up some fresh threads for the cool temperatures and inclement weather ahead.

entry.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Apple Watch Series 12: Every Difference Detailed!
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 watches are both incredibly similar, and surprisingly different – depending on your perspective. Yes, at a high level, the Ultra 4 is bigger (with a bigger battery), better GPS, satellite messaging, emergency siren, deeper dive capabilities, and plenty more. But at the same time, the two units share virtually every software feature – even things like the new Max Extended battery mode launched this year, Audio Intelligence, the internal processors, and more.

Thus, this list is all about helping you figure out what’s the same, and what’s different – and most critically: Whether those specific things matter to you.

You can already see my full Apple Watch Ultra 4 In-Depth Review here, and my Series 12 review is coming up very shortly (and you can find all my Series 12 accuracy data already in my Ultra 4 review too!).

Still, since announce of both watches, I’ve been wearing them side-by-side. Or rather, one per wrist, to see exactly how they differ. As a result, I’ve gathered 50+ features and how they compare. Some of these are big-ticket (or obvious) ones, like battery capacity differences and extra buttons. While others are more subtle, such as the differences in the speakers and microphones. Or how the display panels differ.

With that, let’s dive right into it!

The Pricing:

For most people, the price will be the main deciding factor. It’s also honestly the simplest one: The Ultra 4 is essentially double the price of the Series 12, at least at the base model. Once you start getting into bigger sizes though, and cellular, and other case types (like ceramic), the price difference quickly evaporates.

Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (42mm): $399USD
Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (46mm): $449USD
Apple Watch Ultra 4 (Titanium): $799USD (5G feature included)

Note that for the Apple Watch Series 12 Titanium or Series 12 Ceramic editions, those are only available with cellular. And for the Ultra 4, that comes with cellular as the only option.

Speaking of which, on the Series 12, if you want the cellular editions, they are:

Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (42mm 5G/cellular): $499
Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (46mm 5G/cellular): $549
Apple Watch Series 12 Titanium (42mm cellular): $699
Apple Watch Series 12 Titanium (46mm cellular): $749
Apple Watch Series 12 Ceramic (42mm cellular): $899
Apple Watch Series 12 Ceramic (46mm cellular): $949

As with most years, there are a slate of new bands for all the new units, both the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. In the case of the Series 12, that includes new Nike bands, and in the case of the Ultra 4, that includes new fabric bands and new translucent ocean bands. In most of this review I’ve been wearing the Black Titanium Ultra 4 with the purple Trail band. While the Series 12 I’ve been wearing is the 46mm bronze one.

So with the financial bits out of the way, let’s dive right into the differences beyond the wallet.

The Hardware Differences:

While software can change over time, the hardware won’t. Thus, everything in this section will be the way it is forever with your watch. And honestly, that’s where almost all of the differences are. As always when purchasing, try and decide whether or not a feature actually matters to you today/now, versus something that maybe-kinda-sorta might matter, versus something that you really wish you had.

Meaning, for me I’ll take the bigger battery life of the Ultra 4 over the swankier titanium case or ceramic case on a Series 12, for essentially the same price. Whereas my wife would choose the opposite.

In any case, here we go:

– Ultra 4 has a 49mm case size; Series 12 comes in either a 42mm or 46mm case size
– Ultra 4 stock case is titanium, whereas Series 12 base case is aluminum (with both Titanium & Ceramic case options at a premium price)
– Ultra 4 has a dedicated ‘Action’ button for quick actions
– Ultra 4 has ‘Precision Start’ for workout modes, versus 3-second countdown in Series 12
– Ultra 4 has satellite messaging capability (emergency SOS, text messages, FindMy location sharing)
– Ultra 4 has cellular built-in on all models, whereas Series 12 only in certain models
– Ultra 4 gets ~2.5 days battery life in the real world, Series 12 gets ~1-1.5 days (or 84hrs vs 38hrs in Low Power Mode. Officially, the regular battery life is 50 hours and 24 hours.
– Ultra 4 has GPS battery life of 18 hours, Series 12 is 10 hours
– Ultra 4 has GPS ‘Extended’ battery life of 25 hours, Series 12 is unclaimed
– Ultra 4 has GPS ‘Max Extended’ battery life of 45 hours, Series 12 is unclaimed.
– Ultra 4 has depth gauge to 40m/131ft, Series 12 to only 6m/20ft
– Ultra 4 has depth gauge certified for scuba diving (and meets EN13319 standard), Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 has water resistance to 100m, versus 50m for Series 12
– Ultra 4 has 86dB emergency siren, Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 has multiband/dual-frequency GPS/GNSS, Series 12 has regular GPS/GNSS
– Ultra 4 has three microphones, versus Series 12 has one microphone
– Ultra 4 has dual speakers, Series 12 has a single speaker (but there’s no audible difference in my tests)
– Ultra 4 has sapphire crystal display, and Series 12 base has CeramicShield 2, which Apple says is 60% tougher than the Ion-X glass on the Series 11.
– Ultra 4 display max brightness is 3,000 nits, Series 12 max brightness is 2,000 nits
– Ultra 4 display area is a smidge bigger at 1,245sq mm, vs 1196sq mm (46mm) and 970sqmm (42mm)
– Ultra 4 has a fully flat screen display top, whereas Series 12 has glass curves on edges
– Ultra 4 case weight is 63g (natural/black), versus 38-52g (46mm), and 32-42g (42mm)
– Ultra 4 case thickness is 12mm, versus 9.7mm for Series 12
– Ultra 4 case has button guard around Digital Crown & Button, Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 has been validated to MIL-STD 810H standards, Series 12 has not
– Ultra 4 has an operating temperature of –4° to 113° F (–20° to 45° C), whereas Series 12 is 32° to 95° F (0° to 35° C)
– Ultra 4 has an expanded altimeter range of -1,600ft to 29,500ft (-500m to 9,000m), whereas Series 12 is 0 feet to 10,000 feet (0m to 3000m)
– Ultra 4 has a ceramic & zirconia crystal back case, Series 12 has an aluminum or titanium with a zirconia back case
– Ultra 4 Black has a protective DLC coating on the titanium, whereas neither Ultra 4 (natural/grey) nor Series 12 have DLC
– Ultra 4 fast charges to 80% in 45 minutes, but Series 12 does 80% in 30 minutes
– Ultra 4 fast charges to 18hrs worth in 15 minutes, but Series 12 does 12hrs in 15 minutes
– Both Ultra 4 & Series 12 can do 10hrs of sleep data in 5 minutes of charging

Most of these are self-explanatory, but a few might need some additional explanation/expansion:

– Two-way Satellite Messaging: This was introduced in the Ultra 3, and includes basically three core features. The first is emergency SOS via satellite (if outside of cellular range), the second is text messaging via satellite, and lastly, the ability to update your FindMy location via satellite. This does have some coverage limitations; currently, about 17 countries are supported for Emergency SOS & FindMy (the US, Canada, and most of Europe). However, for iMessage support, it doesn’t support Europe – just United States, Canada, Mexico, and Japan.

– 1 Mic vs 3 Mics: The Series 12 has a single mic and then uses the S11 SIP chipset to do audio voice isolation when calling from the watch, despite having only a single microphone. Whereas the Ultra 4 has three mics, so it can do the majority of that in hardware, but it will still take advantage of the just-added S11 SIP as well to improve that even further. Additionally, with these three microphones, it can do wind cancellation better.

– 1 Speaker vs 2 Speakers: Both watches can play music back these days (without headphones), as well as, of course, a wide variety of other tones/notifications/sounds. Now, despite the Series 12 only having a single speaker, it seemed just as loud for music in my side-by-side tests as the Ultra 4. There was no apparent difference in quality in my test either. You can see the decibel testing side-by-side in my video.

– Multiband/Dual-Frequency GPS vs Regular GPS: There’s nobody who will dive into GPS accuracy testing as deeply (or stupidly) as I do. In most of my tests, these are mostly a wash. Still, if you’re a bit of a nitpicker (like me), there’s definitely a difference between the Ultra 4 (with multiband) and the Series 12 (without it), where the Series 12 will occasionally be just offset or slightly incorrect. It’s rarely a big deal or meaningful, but it is something you can notice.

– Case Thickness: I just want to put this somewhere, but neither the Series 12 nor the Ultra 4 changed external case dimensions this year. So those remain the same as last year, with obviously the Ultra 4 being chunkier than the Series 12 (per the exact specs above). Note that the case thickness excludes the optical HR sensor bump.

– Display Differences: Both displays have the same LTPO3 OLED display introduced first on the Series 10, and now on both Ultra 4 & Series 12 (there were no display changes this year for either watch). This improves so-called off-angle viewing. However, the Ultra 4 has a 3,000 nit display, whereas the Series 12 has a 2,000 nit display. Let’s be clear: Both displays are well beyond overkill for even the sunniest of days (I live on an island in the Mediterranean), you won’t have any issues seeing either. The only notable difference related to the display is that the Ultra has a flat-display cover (lens), whereas the Series 12 has a domed display cover. But I don’t see any difference in real-world visibility either way there.

The official dimensions for the units are:

Series 12 (42mm): 374 by 446 pixels (989 sq mm display area)
Series 12 (46mm): 416 by 496 pixels (1220 sq mm display area)
Ultra 4 (49mm): 422 by 514 pixels (1245 sq mm display area)

When it comes to battery life, the TLDR is the Ultra 4 will get you 2-ish days, whereas the Series 12 will get you 1 strong day. At least in normal smartwatch mode. It’s as simple as that. Both received slight battery increases this year, in sports mode, via the new ‘Extended’ and ‘Max Extended’ modes. As well as slight increases in GPS battery life over last year (from 8-10 hours on Series 12, and from 14 to 18 hours on Ultra 4)

As for the GPS battery life, here are the specs per Apple:

Apple Watch Series 12: 10 hours outdoors GPS (they don’t publish Extended GPS power specs)
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 18 hours outdoors GPS, 25 hours Extended mode GPS, 45 Hours Max Extended GPS mode

Thus far in my testing of both units, the battery claims are holding (at least for regular GPS modes). I’ve covered this in my Ultra 4 In-Depth Review, and will do the same in my upcoming Series 12 In-Depth Review.

The Software Differences:

There are very few differences here, but there are a couple:

– Ultra 4 has Modular & Waypoints watch face, Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 watch face has night mode (goes to a red coloring), Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 allows up to 7 data fields per sport mode setting, whereas Series 12 allows 6 fields. Note this includes the time in the upper right corner
– Ultra 4 has Precision Start (using the Action button), though I’d argue that’s a software feature and not really a hardware feature, hence why I’m including it in both places

Again, this excludes software features dependent on hardware features from the previous section. For example, scuba diving modes require the better depth gauge of the Ultra 4, and satellite messaging requires the redesigned antenna of the Ultra 4, and so on…

Beyond that, it’s all identical across the board.

Things That Are The Same:

One could basically surmise that everything else is the same, and that’s essentially true. Nonetheless, I want to call many of these out, just to illustrate that they are indeed, the same:

– Both run WatchOS 27
– Both have the new heart rate sensing system, which is identical
– Both support the new Audio Intelligence features of Instant Shazam, Sound Recognition, and then later this year Siri Recap and Siri Rewind
– Both have the new HRV recording features
– Both have the new Readiness Scores
– Both get access to all the new Apple Health app features that are coming here shortly.
– Both models have full access to Workout Buddy, and all the other sports features
– Both have offline Siri introduced with the S9 chipset (and now on S11 chipset too)
– Both have features like Double Tap and Wrist Flick
– Both have Blood Oxygen capability
– Both have ECG, Sleep Apnea features, wrist temperature, and all other health metrics
– Both have the Sleep Score, and Hypertension Detection features
– Both have all the same sport modes (as listed in the Workout app)
– Both can do snorkeling via the Depth gauge (and Oceanic+ app), but only Ultra 4 does full diving
– Both have the Compass app, Backtrack, Offline Maps, etc (these are all WatchOS features)
– Both can play back music on their speakers
– Both have a minimum display brightness of 1 nit
– Both have an LTPO wide-angle viewing display, just different top-glass & sizes
– Both have 64GB of internal storage
– Both have a 4-core Neural engine (S11)
– Both have the S11 SIP (chipset)
– Both units have a secondary antenna that they can use for low-signal cases
– Both have a water temperature sensor
– Both units come with a wide variety of stock/base bands, even fabric ones as default options

See, there ya go, it’s not too messy!

As with last year, some of you might ask my preference – and it’s relatively simple: I use the Ultra watches over the Series watches. The reasoning is mostly battery-focused, and simply having to charge one less thing (in my gigantic pile of things). Secondarily, I do appreciate at least the option of having Emergency SOS on my wrist, even if the iMessage piece doesn’t really work for me (yet?) here in Europe.

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Competition: Win a Wahoo Kickr Core 2 turbo trainer worth £500

Cyclist
Competition: Win a Wahoo Kickr Core 2 turbo trainer worth £500

With winter on the way, the perfect partner to keep you riding is the Wahoo Kickr Core 2 turbo trainer. It’s simple to set up, solid, accurate and compatible with your favourite training apps, and best of all, we’ve got one to give away to one lucky reader, just answer this simple question in the form below and sign up to the Cyclist newsletter before 20th October 2026 (hint: we’ll have more competitions on the way so stay tuned).*

What are the names of Wahoo’s bike computers?

A. Bolt, Roam, Ace
B. Strike, Wander, Star
C. Flash, Stone, Joker

entry.title: Readers’ Rides: Pierre’s Raleigh Royal Custom
entry.content:
Pierre from Bike Felix sent in a wonderful Readers’ Rides submission of his Raleigh Royal Custom. Let’s check it out!

I always wanted to have only one bike; I love bikes too much to allow myself to own too many. But having one single bike is truly a hard thing to achieve, as cycling has so much to offer and each bike can really bring out a whole different experience.

This was my brief when I started to build this bike almost 5 years ago now. Back then I was hunting for a vintage touring frame build with reputable tubing and with more clearance than the usual 25/28c found on most vintage bikes. The candidate ended up being this lovely Raleigh Royal from 1988. I bought the frame and started my hunt for the parts.

The build took a long time. I wanted every part to be right and for once I didn’t want to do a period correct restoration but bring a few exotic components. I transferred most of the parts from my previous iteration of the “perfect bike”, a Peugeot PF10 which ended up being too roadie for my taste.

I wanted to keep a classic look while using some modern components. By modern, I mean components still available new today. Do not expect any Shimano DI2 or any other bulky all-black derailleur here. I went all silver and polished, not only because, to me, it looks gorgeous, but in my experience it is also easier to clean.

The transmission uses a Sugino PX crankset with my favourite BCD the 50.4. Gearing-wise, it is a 2×10 with a 42-26T at the front and an 11-32T cassette on the back. I always get confused with gear ratios, so I just tried a few different combinations until this one, which feels right. The shifting is operated with Simplex retroshifters, still my favourite friction shifters to this day, and they are mounted on Gevenalle Gran Compe brake levers. The derailleurs are Microshift R10, picked because they are polished and kinda look classic.

Wheels were hand-built by VeloDuo (a UK bike shop), and I had to go for high flanges for the look; the hubs are Sun XCD with Velo Orange rims. And tyres are Fairweather For CX in that lovely green colour, and obviously tanwall!

The handlebar is a lovely Nitto B135 AA Randonneur, super comfy and slightly flared, and the bar tape is Ergon, matching the tire color perfectly. I also added a front and rear rack for when I go on longer rides and need to carry more stuff; the front is a BLB and the rear is a Nitto R10. There are a lot of smaller cool parts, such as the VO Modernist bottle cages or the MKS Gordito pedals, but I will list the tech specs at the end so you can deep dive into every component.

This bike gets ridden all around the UK; it’s my go-to adventure bike, whether it’s a day ride in the forest, a small bikepacking trip, or even a city ride to the other end of London. I’ve been on many New Forest trips, and with those new gravel tires it really handles more serious gravel than before. I love this bike, my only wish would be bigger tyres, but maybe one day I will convert it to 650B who knows!

Here is the full spec sheet for those who care about this…

Build Spec:

Tubing: Full Reynolds 531 ST
Transmission: Microshift R10
Brake/Shifters: Gevenalle Gran Compe with Simplex retroflection shifters
Brake Calipers: Dia Compe DC980
Crankset: Sugino PX with Specialites TA 26-42
Wheels: Custom-made High Flange SunXCD MK2 Hubs with Velo Orange Enterprise 32H rim
Tyres: Fairweather for CX 700x32c
Cassette: Shimano 10-speed 11-32T
Saddle: Brooks Cambium C17 Carved
Seatpost: Fluted unbranded
Headset: Tange Levin CD
Stem: Nitto Technomic
Handlebar: Nitto B135 AA Randonneur – 450mm
Bartape: Ergon BT Gravel
Bottom bracket: Shimano UN55
Pedals: MKS Gordito
Chain: KMC 10 Speed
Bottle Cages: VO Modernist
Front Rack: BLB
Rear rack: Nitto R10
Cable housing: Nissen

 

 

We’d like to thank all of you who submitted Readers Rides builds to be shared here at The Radavist. The response has been incredible, and we have so many to share over the next few months. Feel free to submit your bike, listing details, components, and other information. You can also include a portrait of yourself with your bike and your Instagram account! Please shoot landscape-orientation photos, not portrait. Thanks!

entry.title: Pinarello Opens First U.S. Bottega in New York City
entry.content:
Pinarello has opened its first Bottega outside Europe, planting a new flagship store at 114 Wooster Street in New York City’s SoHo neighborhood.

The new space joins existing Pinarello Bottegas in London, Zurich, and Villorba, Italy, and gives the brand a USA showcase for its bikes, custom program, and a few pieces of racing history. Think of it as a Pinarello flagship store.

Pinarello Lands in SoHo

The New York Bottega carries Pinarello’s full range, including the recently launched DOGMA X and X Series, with dedicated space for bike fitting, service, and custom consultations.

A major part of the store centers on Pinarello’s MyWay program, which lets customers customize both the paint and specifications of their frame.

Pinarello is positioning its Bottega stores as the full brand experience rather than a traditional dealer floor packed wall-to-wall with inventory. Plus, the brand will do some activations out of the store (new products, etc.) and we’re guessing some rides with Pinarello athletes when available.

“For us, a Bottega is more than just a store,” said Pinarello president Fausto Pinarello. “It is a space where cyclists can truly immerse themselves in our bikes, products and services, and experience the artistry that goes into every frame.”

That approach makes plenty of sense in SoHo, where bike shopping can sit pretty comfortably alongside high-end fashion and design. Just don’t expect to see this the creation above anytime soon.

More Than Just Pinarello Bikes

The new store also has dedicated areas for a handful of Pinarello-adjacent brands. Q36.5 cycling apparel and footwear gets its own space, along with Amacx sports nutrition and Partington carbon wheels.

There’s some proper bike-nerd material in there too.

One standout piece is Filippo Ganna’s Bolide F HR 3D, the bike used for his World Hour Record. If you’ve only ever seen photos of that thing, it’s probably worth stopping in for a closer look. That mix of current product and racing history gives the store a little more personality than a standard retail setup.

Wanna Visit?

The new Bottega gives Pinarello four flagship locations worldwide and its first in the United States. The newest location is:

Pinarello Bottega New York
114 Wooster Street
SoHo, New York City

For anyone who wants to see the latest DOGMA in person, spend some time with the MyWay configurator, or just stare at Ganna’s Hour Record bike for a while, the new SoHo store now gives Pinarello a proper home base in New York.

entry.title: Firefly’s All Road Rim Brake Clears a 700 x 40 mm Tire
entry.content:
Looking forward while simultaneously working backward, Firefly just unveiled a juicy All Road model that clears a 700 x 40 mm tire with modified Cane Creek eeBrake road calipers…

Sometimes framebuilders’ innovations or designs are driven by customer needs. Other times, it’s to match modern components or tech demands. Builders these days are flooded with requests for more tire clearance, more chainring clearance, and faster geometries, which is what led Firefly to develop its 3D-printed chainstay yokes and seat tube knuckles, for example.

No one was asking Firefly for a new rim brake model in 2026. But the Melrose, Massachusetts-based builders still believe in the value of the simplicity of rim brakes. The brand, renowned for exquisitely practical titanium models, realized it had all of the tools it needed to build a modern, versatile, beautiful new all-Ti rim brake bike, and duh, they couldn’t resist. All that it required was closing a few design gaps.

The benefits of bigger tires on road and all-road bikes are undeniable, so Firefly developed a new Ti All Road fork for medium-reach caliper brakes and 40 mm tire clearance.

Firefly worked with Cane Creek to modify their spectacular Brompton eeBrakes with a traditional cable pull, giving the makers a top-of-the-line caliper brake with All Road tire clearance.

Good quick releases are hard to find now, and don’t work well with the Ti fork design to begin with, so Firefly created a new 3D-printed through-bolt dropout design that is lighter and stiffer than older plate dropouts, secures the wheels better than quick releases, and looks beautiful.

The result is a versatile, light, elegant, and modern All Road bike with the simplicity of caliper rim brakes.

It’s not for everyone, naturally, but that’s the beauty of custom bikes; they can speak to niche audiences.

See this stunning bike in more detail at Firefly and see it in person at this weekend’s Crafted Bike Show.

entry.title: Circles Japan Visit Stinner Frameworks
entry.content:
In the latest video from Stinner Frameworks, the team sits down with Shige from Circles Japan and Sim Works during his visit to Stinner’s Santa Barbara workshop.

In this video, Aaron and Shige discuss their new partnership bringing Stinner Frameworks custom hand-built bicycles to Japan. Shige shares the story of Circles, from its origins in Nagoya nearly 20 years ago to the opening of Circles Tailored, a shop dedicated to custom handmade bikes.

The video dives into Japanese cycling culture—from everyday commuting (Mama Chari) to the growing popularity of bikepacking and gravel riding, while discussing Sim Works, Circles’ iconic in-house components brand showcasing Japanese craftsmanship with brands like Nitto, Honjo, and Panaracer.

entry.title: The Leatt Limited Nukeproof Axess Racing Capsule Collection
entry.content:
Leatt is celebrating an exciting season with the Nukeproof Axess Racing (NAR) team by releasing a limited-edition capsule collection. As the 2026 World Cup enters its final phase, one thing is clear: nothing compares to the unbridled emotion of downhill racing. Leatt harnesses this energy with a radical creative direction that’s become the distinctive livery of the NAR team.

The team livery draws it’s inpsiration from the euphoric energy of 1990s rave culture and the excitement of the modern World Cup downhill circuit. “Downhill racing isn’t simply about performance,” says Mille Johnset, NAR’s standout Norwegian rider. “It’s the stoke, the chaos, the community. There’s so much passion for this sport everywhere we go. Wearing this gear is a signal to the world that we’re not afraid to have fun!

A small, limited collection of casual apparel is now available. Featuring all four NAR team designs, these t-shirts, long sleeves, hoody and cap are the same as those the team has been wearing in their downtime this season.

The limited capsule collection is available today at Leatt.

entry.title: Steel Is Still Real: Ritchey’s Road Logic Returns with Tom’s Autograph, Right on the Top Tube
entry.content:
Some cool news out of San Carlos, California. It seems that Ritchey Design is bringing back the Road Logic Frameset. This time, it’s the Signature Edition, with Tom himself putting his name right there on the top tube. The frame is beautiful and covered in Ritchey Classic Red.

Tom Ritchey has been bending, brazing, and welding steel tubes since before some of us were born; I mean, not me, but some of us. And having his signature on this particular frame is actually making a statement, and not some marketing trick.

The statement is a “yeah, I stand behind this one” kind of statement. There is something very beautiful about a skinny-tubed, svelte road bike frame. Look, I don’t even ride road anymore, but I would love to build this frame up.

Steel is Still Real…

Ritchey Design Marketing Director explains, “There is still real demand for high-quality rim-brake steel road framesets. Devotees of such bikes know that this special Road Logic will deliver on the promise of a ride feel that moves the soul of its pilot. And they’re going to love seeing Tom’s signature on the top tube.”

The new Ritchey Road Logic uses Tom’s own heat-treated, triple-butted Logic tubeset, with short-butted sections specifically tuned for TIG welding. Tom’s attention to detail when frame building after fifty-plus years in the game is either admirable obsession or just what happens when framebuilding is literally in your actual blood. Either way, I think it’s the good kind of stubborn.

The new Ritchey Road Logic is spec’d with Ritchey’s carbon fork. A carbon fork on a steel frame is a great idea to keep overall weight to a minimum. But it’s also great for some vibration damping and steering precision. Not to mention, the fork allows for tire clearance up to 30c tires.

Combine the lightweight steel tubset, bigger tires, and a carbon fork, and you get a steel bike doing what a steel bike does best… smooth out bad pavement while still snapping back when you stand up and sprint. The new Ritchey Road Logic is built for the long haul, but not scared to deliver the juice when you ask it to.

The Geometry

Ritchey Road Logic Retail & Detail

Retail: $1,759

  • Sizes: 49, 51, 53, 55, 57, 59cm
  • Heat-treated, triple-butted Ritchey Logic tubeset
  • TIG-welded
  • Ritchey full carbon fork
  • 700x30c tire clearance (depending on tire/rim manufacturer)
  • Headset: WCS drop-in 1-1/8” (included)
  • Weight: 1.77kg (55cm – frame-only)

If you are a cyclist who’s been faithful to the good ol’ rim-brake, this is a nice reminder that some builders are still making bikes that are “simple and light. No discs, no calipers to bleed, no hydraulic lines, and no extra weight. Just a beautiful frame doing its job.

RitcheyLogic.com

entry.title: In the Drops: Albion’s patchwork Ultralight jersey and thermal bib shorts, Keela’s jazzy Raincoat, Cervélo’s racy Soloist and Ravemen’s beefed up lights
entry.content:
Cyclist
In the Drops: Albion’s patchwork Ultralight jersey and thermal bib shorts, Keela’s jazzy Raincoat, Cervélo’s racy Soloist and Ravemen’s beefed up lights

It’s nearly Worlds time – a reason to celebrate but also a reason to mourn. It’s almost the end of the season. Before we know it, Hill Climb season will be upon us and I’ll be getting tricked into doing one in pursuit of editorial excellence. To keep up with the final spate of pro action we’ve got a Q&A with Michael Storer from the magazine, a World’s Road Race form guide and a Pro Log roundup from Robyn.

In the world of performance apparel, big moves are afoot too. After dusting off the wallet and buying Bristol-based luggage company Tailfin, Castelli has updated its iconic Gabba and Perfetto lines to include the Polartec AirCore Fabric. I’ve tested it elsewhere, and it is effective stuff. Reviews of Oakley’s banned Meta glasses, Scott’s new Addict, and Scribe’s Elan Ultra 5 wheels are all live too.

It’s very nice to see some dedicated bikepacking content on the site too. Expert guide Emma Karslake has outlined her recommendations for bikepacking in Europe, which includes tips for packing and the best destinations. And if you get really reeled in, some races too.

Now for a gentle descent into the drops.

Albion Ultralight Insulated Jacket and ABR1 Thermal Pocket bib shorts

British endurance specialist Albion isn’t afraid to try out original designs in its quest to equip riders for the weirdest and most changeable weather imaginable. That means events like the Atlas Mountain Race, where it can be upwards of 35°C in the daytime, and sub-zero at night.

The Ultralight Insulated jacket is an unerring whisp of kit. The fabric used for the body and arms is Quantam NetPlus from Pertex. Full marks for the scientific name, but what does it actually do? Albion says it’s been chosen for the new iteration of this jersey because of its light weight but is also 100% recycled from fishing nets and fully traceable. I can attest that it definitely doesn’t smell of fish either.

The main design choice that sets it apart from other garments is the patched insulation. Albion has sewn Primaloft Gold Cross Core insulation into the upper arms and torso of the Ultralight – a change from the last version. When you hold it up to the light, it’s very clear to see the difference, with the insulated sections clearly protecting the rider from the worst buffetings of cold wind.

‘The ultralight insulated jacket is all about warmth to weight, and packability,’ says Charlie Stewart, co-founder and head of Product. ‘A men’s medium weighs about 96 grams, and it’s a jacket that just disappears into a pocket or a frame pack when not being used. The jacket uses a 40gsm Primaloft Cross Core insulation, technology originally developed by NASA to maximise warmth-to-weight, and it’s become a core item in the packing lists of bike packers and ultra racers all over the world.’

(No one’s asking me, but surely extra weight in a gravity-free vehicle doesn’t really matter? You have my details NASA).

Albion has made a few other changes to the jacket, adding an elastic hem gripper and cuffs, different sizes for men and women and an internal mesh pocket for stashing the entire jacket into. It packs down into a hand-sized bundle.

Elsewhere, Albion’s very well-reviewed ABR1 bib shorts now have an insulated option too. ‘We’ve retained the premium Italian knitted performance fabrics, our signature three-pocket cargo system, a pad by Elastic Interface for long distance riding and in our women’s version a strap system for easy comfort breaks – whilst making them useable in cold weather,’ says Stewart. ‘The shorts use Thermoroubaix fabric by Miti Spa, a highly insulating, durable brushed back fabric with stretch, and for the pockets a brushed back grid fleece fabric for additional insulation. When used with our new Leg Warmers, the temperature range for these shorts can stretch from near freezing into the mid teens.’

If you’re not a fan, Albion offers a 60-day return on used bibs so you can exchange them for an alternative or a refund. I’m usually a Large in Albion kit, but a medium fitted just fine here, so it’s worth paying a bit of attention to the sizing grid.

  • Buy now from Albion (£195 and £205)

Keela Raincoat

You can see where I’m going with this. Surely these blue skies are heading elsewhere soon. Well, when they do, Keela has got you sorted. Its new Aeroshell Jacket, available in two very fetching shades of ultramarine (blue) and ignition (orange), is suited for a range of different outdoor pursuits, including cycling.

The material incorporates its Flylite Dri Fabric, which is said to be both waterproof and breathable, allowing sweat and moisture to escape before you overheat. Handily, the hood is specially scooped out so that it fits over the top of a helmet, and can be rolled away when out of use. The zips Keela has fitted are all waterproof too, sealing up the entire package.

The sizing range is massive, running from XS to 3XL, and the whole thing packs down pretty small, so it can live happily in a backpack when commuting or a seatpost or frame bag when out on a proper ride.

  • Buy now from Keela (£129.95)

Ravemen FR1500 and CL200 lights

Personally, the time of year doesn’t affect my attitude towards lights. It’s lights on, whatever the time, whatever the month. I can’t count the number of times I’ve seen drivers take a furtive look in their rear-view mirror at the sight of my flashing beam, just as their reaching arm (not indicator light) tells me they’re about to come charging left across the bus lane and bosh me into next week.

The coming autumn signals more people using lights, more of the time. So it’s just as well that Ravemen has updated its highest-strength FR1500 front light. Ravemen is known for lights that have both a male and female computer mount fitting, meaning you can mount your computer on top of the 270° light. And that handy detail hasn’t changed, but a number of things have been updated.

There is a more refined build quality this time around, including additional heat-dissipating fins – 1500 lumens is the brightest light Ravemen does and it gets hot! A cable is included so the light doubles as a 3500 mAh power bank if your computer is on the brink. That light has a range of up to 115 metres and includes an increased range of beam patterns but will last on its own for a claimed 60 hours depending on usage.

This model (not the SE model) also includes an out-front mount that fits onto a round handlebar. My kingdom for a company that can make a universal out front mount. I must have about ten kicking around my draw, barely any of which fit any bike other than the one it’s specifically intended for. Unfortunately, none of the bikes I currently have in my possession has round handlebars so the photographs aren’t in situ.

Its natural companion at the rear is the new CL200 tail light. This is designed to point out longways at a horizontal angle mirroring the visibility of the front light. It’s smart too, with the internal monitor highlighting the light when it detects braking or abrupt deceleration. Ravemen claims it is 300° for the rear light. Both lights have some decent waterproofing too.

In terms of attachment, it fits to rails or onto seat posts, including some longer aero seat posts, and these come in the box. Ravemen claims a 160-hour slow flashing run time on the 31g light which should do most people for a good few weeks of riding. Now, let’s go and see about this rave.

  • Buy now from Ravemen (£94.95 & £54.95)

Cervélo Soloist

I’ve only had Cervélo’s updated Soloist on loan for a week, but I’ve been impressed so far. I was lucky enough to test the last one back in 2023 and things have moved on quite significantly with big 36mm clearance, aero bottle cages, more integration, and a more refined profile.

Unlike some other brands, Cervélo is still intent on producing a triumvirate of WorldTour grade road bikes, with the Soloist filling the gap between the hella aero S5 and the hella lightweight R5. But this is no compromise bike. No sir. Cervélo claims it’s faster than the Tarmac SL8 in the wind tunnel and only a whisker over 7kg even in this 1x SRAM Force AXS build with a beefcake XPLR rear derailleur. That’s thanks to a general chipping away at every tube and join, although surface area is actually up overall.

That said, it’s not a whole lot cheaper, ringing up at £7,000 in this spec. That’s the same price as the Factor Monza, which was positioned as a more accessible race bike, albeit with the emphasis heavily on aero. The Soloist is lighter and, if the claims are true, potentially more aero too especially with a 1x setup.

Depending on your dint, other changes might charm or grate. Like the Aethos 2 I tested recently, Cervélo has moved the cockpit to totally internal routing with a spacer arrangement that perhaps isn’t the most straightforward I’ve encountered. But don’t worry, those aero bottle cages take normal bidons too.

Aesthetically, the changes are clear. As seems to be the general direction of travel, the frontal area is far smaller but the side on profile is larger. Are we moving into the Flat Stanley era of bikes, and away from chubbier tubing? It does seem that way.

Keep your eyes out for more on the Soloist in the magazine as we’ve got a studio feature and then a full in-depth review to follow. My comments about the decidedly inoffensive colourways might not make the edit in print so I’ll express my indifference here while I can. Come on bike brands, we can do better than white or black surely? Yes, there’s a fresh turquoise frameset available but frankly, that’s not enough.

  • Buy now from Sigma Sports (£7,000)

What we’re into this week: Audax

The end of summer means a wild scrabble to fit in a final Audax or two before things get really filthy out there. For me that means the 200km Saints and Sinners ride, which is running from St Albans to Bury St Edmunds and back again. Inevitably this will lead curmudgenous web editor Will Strickson to berate me once more that ‘anything less than 300km isn’t an Audax’, but since I’m yet to see him crack three figures this summer, I won’t let his critiques damage my morale too much.

As you’d expect for that neck of the woods, it’s a mercifully flat one. That means packing the Soloist, rather than the Aethos, and teeing up some nice aero bits and pieces to go with it. A firm favourite for sportives this summer has been the Apidura Aero Bags, which I featured last year. They’re just the same as a frame bag but designed in such a way that a delightfully smooth join around the head tube/top tube junction is created, like the bags Canyon fits to the Grail and claims are more aero on than off. You can believe it.

The rest of the kit hasn’t come together yet, but it could be some shoulder season business. I’m thinking the thermal Albion bib shorts and some kind of long sleeve arrangement to go with it. Plus I’ll be cooking up some oaty/ricecakey business the night before, so please do let me know of any recipes that work well.

The post In the Drops: Albion’s patchwork Ultralight jersey and thermal bib shorts, Keela’s jazzy Raincoat, Cervélo’s racy Soloist and Ravemen’s beefed up lights appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Norco Revives the Team DH with New Six-Link Suspension
entry.content:
After several years of absence, Norco has announced the return of the Team DH downhill bike. A full-bred race machine designed to take Norco’s team riders to the podium, the new Team DH was fine-tuned with input from racers Greg Minaar, Danny Hart and Gracey Hemstreet. After five years of development on the World Cup Circuit and many design revisions, the bike launches today with some clever features to show.

Most notably, the new Team DH debuts Norco’s new HVP6 six-link suspension linkage. This downhill-specific linkage features adjustable progressivity and adjustable anti-squat via two idler positions. To ensure a proper fit, the bike also includes reach-adjustable headset cups and size-specific rear ends. The Team DH was designed to remain stable and composed on the track, hold lines through rough terrain, and allow the rider to find speed wherever possible.

Norco Team DH – Construction Features:

The new Team DH is built around an aluminum front triangle and a carbon rear end. The aluminum front provides optimal stiffness and durability, while the carbon rear is tuned to find traction and offer a responsive ride while reducing unsprung mass. The bike features 200 mm of rear travel and runs MX wheels. Norco makes no mention of full 29” compatibility.

One significant feature of the Team DH is its new HVP6 Suspension linkage – A patented, High Virtual Pivot Six-link layout optimized for downhill racing. Norco says by adding linkage elements between the main suspension system and the shock, they can eliminate inherent compromises of four-bar linkages. The HVP6 linkage offers more tuning control over individual suspension characteristics and how they affect the bike’s braking behaviour, axle path, and leverage curve. The Team DH’s linkage is tuned to stay highly active to absorb repeated high-speed impacts, but remain supportive in corners and composed under hard braking.

Next up is the Team DH’s progression adjustment. Flip-chips at both rear shock eyelets offer two leverage rate curve settings (P+ and P-) to suit different riders, terrain, or track conditions. Both eyelets get flip-chips because the Team DH’s entire shock moves backwards or forwards on the frame to achieve the different rate curves. Norco says this alters the bike’s progression but maintains its initial sensitivity; this enables riders to play with the progression settings without requiring other adjustments to compensate between them. Bikes will ship in the P- position, and switching to the P+ setting increases progressivity by 2.5%.

To allow fine-tuning of anti-squat, Norco gave the Team DH an adjustable idler position, using a patent licensed from i-Track. This provides riders with control over drivetrain response and pedal feedback. Via interchangeable mounting plates and guides, the idler can be set at two positions (AS+ and AS-). Bikes ship in the AS+ setting, and moving to the AS- setting reduces anti-squat by 20%.

Before the rider even starts tuning, the Team DH’s rear shocks are already custom-tuned for each frame size to ensure the bike’s intended kinematics remain consistent for everyone.

As for key fitments, the Team DH features a UDH derailleur hanger, an 83mm threaded BSA bottom bracket, and runs a 148mm Boost rear axle. The frame fits 31.6mm seat posts and includes an ISCG-05 mount.

With race-day maintenance in mind, the Team DH features oversized bearings, low-hassle frame hardware (like top hat spacers), and external cable routing. Norco notes that no special tools are required to work on the Team DH, and service kits will be available so riders can keep their bikes race-ready throughout the season.

As a Norco-specific bonus, buyers can use their Ride Aligned website to help tune their bike’s settings – including the Team DH’s reach, progressivity, and idler position adjustments.

Geometry:

For additional fit tuning, the Team DH comes equipped with reach-adjustable headset cups that allow for neutral, +5, or -5mm positions. They also feature size-specific rear ends, with only the S1 and S2 sharing the same chainstay lengths. The rear end lengths were chosen based on testing with riders on all frame sizes, considering fit and real-world weight distribution measurements. The varying lengths ensure all riders stay centered between the wheels and enjoy consistent balance, grip, and handling. Up front, Norco slacks the head tubes by an additional half a degree on the largest three frame sizes. If you check out the build specs, you’ll notice Norco stocks lower-rise handlebars and shorter cranks on the two smallest frame sizes.

The five available frame sizes (S1 to S5) should fit riders from 5’ to 6’3”. Check out the chart above for all the specs.

Model Lineup:

There will be two complete models of the Team DH, plus a frame kit.

Team DH 2 Fox: $7,999

Check out Norco’s website for full build specs, but here’s a quick rundown of some key components: The Team DH 2 Fox model comes with a Fox 40 Performance Elite 200mm fork and a Factory DHX2 rear shock with a Sprindex spring. This bike gets a SRAM GX DH drivetrain, a Praxis Cadet DH9 crankset, and SRAM Maven base brakes. It rolls on RaceFace ARC HD rims with DT Swiss 370 hubs. The Team DH 2 Fox comes in satin silver/blue.

Team DH 2 RockShox: $7399

For fans of RockShox suspension, this model runs a Boxxer Select D2 200mm fork and a Vivid Coil Base rear shock with a Sprindex spring. It shares the same SRAM GX DH drivetrain and Maven base brakes as the Fox-equipped model, but runs a Praxis Cadet HD crank. The RaceFace/DT Swiss wheelset is the same on both compete models. This bike also comes in satin silver/blue.

Team DH Frame Kit: $4599

The Team DH frame kit includes a Fox Factory DHX2 rear shock with a Sprindex spring, a seat clamp, rear axle, and an MRP G5 SL chain guide. The frame kit is sold in a gloss black/blue colorway.
