entry.title: I’m Over The Moon About 7mesh’s MK3 Cargo Bib Shorts!
entry.content:
Nothing ensures an enjoyable ride like a good chamois that keeps you comfortable in the saddle. When your bibs can also carry snacks, tools, and other items, that’s just icing on the cake! Several years ago I tested 7mesh’s non-bib MK3 shorts, and they are still one of my most comfortable chamois that I typically save for longer rides. With the Cargo Bib version, road or gravel riders can haul a few extra items, and MTB riders can likely ditch their packs.

I tested the MK3 Cargo Bib Shorts on my MTB, and paired with a water bottle, I was able to carry all the essential supplies I’d typically put in a pack with no discomfort or excess bulkiness. Between the absence of a pack and the strap-style uppers, these bibs were a great option for staying cooler on hot rides.

Editor’s note – I hope you chuckle at my ‘cheeky’ photos bookending this post – As an MTB rider reviewing bib shorts, I had to get creative to show you a product that’s entirely hidden while in use! Might as well have some fun with it!

7mesh MK3 Cargo Bib Shorts – Construction Features:

7mesh designs a lot of their clothing to be versatile across different riding styles, and these bib shorts are a great example. The MK3 bibs are equally suitable for road, gravel, or MTB riders. If these bibs were MTB-specific, I’d say a fly would be a great addition to them. However, I wouldn’t expect a fly on bibs that are intended as an outer layer for road/gravel riders.

The MK3 Cargo Bib’s body is made from a Nylon/Elastane fabric blend and was designed to offer moderate compression with a ‘skin fit’. 7mesh’s Clean Finish tailoring keeps seams and stitching away from key areas that can cause discomfort.

These bibs feature the same floating Elastic Interface Performance Space chamois as my older MK3 non-bib shorts, which is great – You shouldn’t mess with a good thing!

The Performance Space chamois features high-density foam in the center channel and a breathable, perforated top layer. Men’s and women’s models get gender specific channels or inserts to avoid pressure points or discomfort. This chamois was designed to remain comfortable for long hours in the saddle.

A significant feature of these bibs is the minimal uppers. The MK3 Cargo bibs have 45mm-wide soft elastic bib straps which leave most of your upper body uncovered. Slim, clean-looking raw hems on the legs support your muscles without feeling like elastic bands, and thin silicone grippers are printed inside to keep them in place. 

As for cargo, the MK3’s offer three back pockets, plus large side pockets on both legs.

7mesh strives to be eco-friendly, so these bibs are made using Bluesign-approved fabric, Oeko-Tex Standard 100 certified fabric, recycled fabric in the chamois, and PFAS-free body fabric. The MK3 Cargo Bibs can be machine washed in cold water, but 7mesh recommends hanging them to dry.

Ride Impressions: Fit/Comfort:

I’ve been riding the MK3 Cargo Bibs since mid-May. I’m 5’ 10” with a slim build, and the size small bibs fit me great. The upper straps are snug but not too tight, and the legs are long but cut off high enough to overlap but not interfere with kneepads. The wide, flat hems on the legs are very comfortable.  

The body and belly cut both fit my torso well. The fit of the body is a bit looser than the waistline of my snug-fitting non-bib MK3 shorts, which is great. If my older MK3s were much tighter, they would not be comfortable.

I like the moderate compression fit of the MK3 bibs, particularly on the legs. My muscles feel very well supported in these shorts: from the lower hems to the body area, everything fits nice and snug. For MTB riders, the snug legs also discourage kneepads from slipping downwards.

While the seams surrounding the chamois are all hidden or minimized, there are some seams inside the hips, legs, and back that aren’t. The seams around the hips left impressions on my skin after each ride, but fortunately none of those unprotected seams caused noticeable discomfort.

After all my test riding, I’ve found the MK3 Cargo Bibs perfectly comfortable all around – there are no issues to report!  

Chamois:

7mesh’s Performance Space chamois is very comfortable, providing excellent saddle padding. Even on my third ride with a new Chromag Limber saddle (which is less padded than the Ergon seat I was riding) I remained comfortable for over three hours.

It’s not a particularly thin chamois, but I don’t find it too thick. It’s substantial enough to keep you comfortable throughout long rides, as intended. The floating construction seems to keep the chamois in position really well, and I never had problems with the chamois shifting around, bunching, or chafing me anywhere.

Straps:

The best thing about the suspender/strap uppers is how cool they are compared to bibs with back panels. I came home from one short, hot ride and realized I wasn’t that sweaty… then remembered I rode without a pack! Being able to carry ride essentials in the bibs, especially for those (like me) without frame storage, allows you to stay much cooler on any ride you can pull off with a water bottle. I avoid wearing bibs in the summertime, but I won’t think twice about wearing the MK3 Cargo Bibs for any ride.

The other thing I liked about the straps is how they remained comfortable when I did ride with a pack. I still wear hydration packs for most rides (and have to carry my camera pack often), and wearing them over the slim straps was never uncomfortable. Even the junction piece between the shoulders was easily forgotten during rides.

Fit With MTB Shorts:

Since I tested the MK3 Cargo Bibs riding MTB, I always wore them with shorts over top. With items in the back pockets, I noticed my Endura shorts had to sit a bit low in the back. I would have pulled up the waist a tad higher, but it was interfering with the pockets. Luckily it was only by a small margin, so my shorts were fine where they were – they didn’t slip down on the ride and the waist wasn’t nearly low enough to restrict motion.

When I wore my Patagonia shorts, they initially sat slightly overlapping the bottoms of the pockets. I loaded up the pockets and rode, and when I got home the shorts’ waistline had settled in just under the pockets. Again, the waist moved downwards so slightly that I didn’t even notice.

Only my pair of Yeti shorts, which have a higher rear waistline, sat over the rear pockets considerably. Thankfully, if you don’t fill the pockets, this overlap isn’t noticeable at all. Most MTB shorts will likely not be problematic with the bibs’ rear pockets… worst-case scenario, you can still wear any shorts with higher waistlines if you leave the pockets empty.

Cargo:

I found the MK3 Cargo Bibs can comfortably carry an impressive amount of essential items. On an early test ride, I put Skittles in one leg pocket, a Clif bar in the other, and quickly forgot about both! The leg pockets hold small items snugly, and those items never sat right underneath the stuff in my shorts’ pockets.

On a couple of rides, I put all the essentials I’d typically carry in a pack in the bibs to see if anything felt obtrusive or annoying. Between the legs and back pockets, I carried a Clif bar, a small multi-tool, a large and a small Co2 canister, a dynaplug tool, a pack of spare plugs, my Co2 inflator head and valve core tool, plus a spare set of batteries for my Archer electronic shifter.

I even tempted fate and put the multi tool in the middle back pocket, right on my spine. While I would say the multi-tool was noticeable, it was never annoying, and it didn’t bounce around on my back while I rode. The worst I can say is that items in the back pockets may be noticeable, depending on what you put in there, but nothing I carried ever became problematic.

Even riding with a pack and shorts with pockets, I put some energy chews in the leg pocket of the cargo bibs just for easy access. It also spread out my phone and the chews instead of shoving both in my shorts’ pocket. I did notice one thing – cargo in those back pockets will get sweaty! Metal items like multi-tools or Co2 inflators might eventually start getting rusty, but I suspect it would take a while.

The MK3 Cargo Bib Short sells for $250. Men’s color options are Black, Deep Sea, or Purple Velvet. Sizes range from XS-XXL. Women’s models are also available: The WK3 Cargo Bib Short retails for $230. Color choices are Black, Midnight Blue, or Peat, and they come in sizes XS-XL.

7mesh.com

entry.title: The State 8-Speed Road Bike is $650 w/ Integrated Shifters! Plus New All Road Flatbar & Exclusive SRAM Aero Cranks
entry.content:
State Bicycle Co. is heading into Fall with some new players to the game, some updates, new colors, and a brand new 4130 8-Speed. This refresh shows that State continues to make really great products at really great prices.

For me, the headliner is the new 4130 8 Speed Road at $649.99. It’s a drop-bar option for people who want a road bike without needing to make a major financing decision. Also crawling out of the past is the 10-Speed All Road Flat Bar, which State’s calling a “complete throwback”.

On the dirt side, the 4130 Trail hardtail arrives in a very handsome Sagebrush Green, and the Raw Phosphate colorway (one of my favorites) is fully restocked.

The Upgrades…

On the exciting upgrade menu is the Seekrun wireless dropper, for which State is the exclusive US distributor. Further up the price ladder, we find that the Carbon All Road v2 gets a pretty Colorado Blue colorway and starts at $2,399.99 complete.

The recently launched Carbon Road, which sold out quickly, is back and starts at a mere $2,799.99 with an aero-focused 1x package and a new crank developed with SRAM that’s exclusive to State. I know a 1x aero road setup won’t shock anyone in 2026. But an exclusive SRAM crank on a bike at this price point? That’s something pretty cool.

Let’s take a look at the goods.

4130 8-Speed Road

Retail: $649.99

Reimagining their best-selling 4130 Fixed Gear, State launches a budget-friendly entry-level road bike. A perfect road bike for getting into road cycling, the commuter, or anyone who wants a fun, affordable ride. It uses a double-butted steel tubeset for the frame and has a classic look.

It uses Sensah Reflex 1×8 integrated shifters and 700c x 38mm tires that can handle all the imperfect roads. The rim brakes keep it light, low-maintenance, and easy to maintain. Using common standards for components means easy sourcing, replacement, and upgrades.

4130 8-Speed Road Features

  • 1 ⅛ Steerer
  • 68mm English Threaded BB Shell
  • Integrated 8-speed Shifters (42t front / 11-28 rear)
  • Double Butted Steel Frame and Fork
  • 38mm Tires
  • Dual Pivot Rim Brakes
  • Colors: Sea Foam / Sapphire & Chrome / Black & Tan

4130 All-Road Flat Bar

Retail: $899.99

This bike slightly resembles the MTB’s of old. I think that’s the charm of the reimagined 4130 Flat Bar. It blends the past with some modern components. For instance, it comes equipped with UDH, Hydraulic disc brakes, and Microshift 10-speed shifting.

Again, State makes a wonderfully simple bike that utilizes common standards. It also has completely external cable routing, which means easy maintenance, repair, and upgrading.

The 4130 Flat Bar has 450mm chainstays across the entire size range. It comes stock with 650b tires that provide clearance for up to 2.4″ tires. For those who prefer a larger wheel, you can run it with 700 x 2.25″ and still have clearance. All of this means a versatile bike for a wide range of uses.

4130 All-Road Flat Bar Features

  • 650 x 2.1 Vittoria Tires
  • UDH Compatibility
  • Hydraulic Disc Brakes
  • Full Chrome Finish Kit
  • Color Options: Black Stone / Schoolyard Yellow / Mint Chocolate Chip

Carbon Road & SRAM 1x Aero

Retail: $2999.99

When State first launched their Carbon Road, the story was a big hit with you guys. It was an incredibly good-looking, serious road bike that was also super affordable. I mean, what’s not to like?

The updated version is spec’d with SRAM Rival shifting, trusted components, and the new custom 1x Aero crank (exclusive to State) from SRAM. A 48-tooth chainring paired with a 13-speed 10-46 cassette is the same stuff the pro peloton runs.

You can also add an Enve wheel upgrade to the Carbon Road, which still only puts the build at $3999.99. Where can you find a value like that? Thanks, State Bikes!

Carbon Road Features

  • Frame Weight: Standard (M) 1100g / SL (M) 820g
  • SRAM Rival Shifting (1x and 2x options)
  • Custom 1x SRAM Aero 48t Crank (State Exclusive)
  • T47 Bottom Bracket
  • Aero Tubing Profiles
  • Multiple upgrade options available

Hit the link below to check out the value that State Bikes offers, or to scoop up one of these cool bikes.

StateBicycle.com

entry.title: UCI World Championships 2026 Women’s Elite Road Race: Our form guide
entry.content:
Cyclist
UCI World Championships 2026 Women’s Elite Road Race: Our form guide

The women’s elite road race at the UCI World Championships takes place on Saturday, with 180.4km to decide who will wear the rainbow jersey in 2027.

After a steady start, the race takes eight laps of the same 13.4km hilly Montreal circuit as the men, with the Voie Camillien-Houde (1.7km, 7.7%) and Côte de Polytechnique (0.8km, 5.7%) ascents.

Last year, Canada’s Magdeleine Vallieres claimed a surprise victory in Rwanda ahead of Niamh Fisher-Black (New Zealand) and Mavi García (Spain), and she’ll be at home this year to try to defend her title, with Montreal just two hours away from where she grew up in Sherbrooke.

Demi Vollering (Netherlands)

European Road Race Champion Demi Vollering has won a lot throughout her career, but the World Championships rainbow bands elude her. This might just be the season that changes however, coming off another ferociously dominant year with two Grand Tours win and collection of Classics riders spend their whole careers chasing, and this punchy Montreal course suits her.

Her closest challenge came in the form of a silver medal in Glasgow in 2023. In 2024, she lost the sprint finish to come fifth, while in 2025 she won the sprint from the group of favourites but they lingered behind six others on the road. She’s unlikely to let a group get away again.

Road victories this season

  • GC, Tour de France Femmes
  • Stage 9, Tour de France Femmes
  • Stage 8, Tour de France Femmes
  • Stage 5, Tour de France Femmes
  • GC, Giro d’Italia Women
  • Stage 8, Giro d’Italia Women
  • Stage 5, Giro d’Italia Women
  • Liège-Bastogne-Liège
  • La Flèche Wallonne Femmes
  • Tour of Flanders
  • Omloop Nieuwsblad
  • GC, Setmana Ciclista Valenciana
  • Stage 4, Setmana Ciclista Valenciana
  • Stage 1, Setmana Ciclista Valenciana

Last five results

  • 8th: World Championship Elite Women Individual Time-Trial
  • 3rd: Vivi Zuricrit
  • 1st overall: Tour de France Femmes
  • 1st: Stage 9, Tour de France Femmes
  • 1st: Stage 8, Tour de France Femmes

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 2nd: 2023

Kim Le Court-Pienaar (Mauritius)

Kim Le Court-Pienaar has made history pretty much every step of her career so far. In 2025 she became the first African rider to win a Monument at Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the first African rider to wear the yellow jersey at the Tour de France Femmes, and then also became the first to win a stage at the race too thanks to her Stage 5 victory.

The Mauritian Champion stormed to another victory at the Tour this year despite having a tough season with injury and also had a spirited GC fight, ending the race ninth overall. Just a few weeks later she carried that form into the Tour of Britain, where she picked up a maiden GC win.

Le Court-Pienaar has an excellent punch and a strong sprint finish, she should place highly here and has a really good chance at taking another famous victory.

Road victories this season

  • GC, Tour of Britain Women
  • Stage 3, Tour of Britain Women
  • Stage 6, Tour de France Femmes
  • Mauritius National Championships, Road Race
  • Mauritius National Championships, Individual Time-Trial

Last five results

  • 12th: World Championship Mixed Relay Team Time-Trial
  • DNF: Classic Lorient Agglomération
  • 1st overall: Tour of Britain Women
  • 26th: Stage 5, Tour of Britain Women
  • 3rd: Stage 4, Tour of Britain Women

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 8th: 2025

Paula Blasi (Spain)

An Amstel Gold Race win. A podium at La Flèche Wallonne. Victory at La Vuelta Femenina. Fifth at the Tour de France Femmes. That’s just a snapshot of the incredible season Spain’s 23-year-old Paula Blasi has had so far. Barely more than a year into her pro career, Blasi been phenomenal to witness and could really do something on a hilly, attritional parcours at the World Championships.

In 2025, Blasi scored third place in the U23 road race, so this will be her elite level debut and she’s on co-leadership duties alongside UAE Team L’Imad teammate Mavi García, who finished third in last year’s race. This pairing could do something special.

Road victories this season

  • GC, Volta Ciclista a Femenina
  • Stage 2, Volta Ciclista a Femenina
  • CIC-Tour Féminin des Pyrénées
  • Durango Durango Emakumeen Saria
  • La Vuelta Femenina
  • Amstel Gold Race

Last five results

  • 6th: World Championship Mixed Relay Team Time-Trial
  • 18th: World Championship Elite Women Individual Time-Trial
  • 2nd: Pointe du Raz Ladies Classic
  • 27th: Tout commence en Finistère Ladies Classic
  • 5th overall: Tour de France Femmes

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • N/A

Lotte Kopecky (Belgium)

Two-time World Champion Lotte Kopecky is utterly dominant at her best, crushing Classics and thriving in punishing conditions. However she hasn’t been at her best in the last two seasons, with her win rate showing just that, decreasing from 16 in 2024 (including the rainbow jersey) to just three as things stand in 2026.

Counting her out would be a dangerous move though. In 2023, she won the road race in a 5.6km solo attack, and in 2024 she won the small group sprint after a brilliant fighting performance and incredible support from Justine Ghekiere.

Road victories this season

  • Stage 4, La Vuelta Femenina
  • Milan-San Remo
  • Danilith Nokere Koerse

Last five results

  • 6th: World Championship Elite Women Individual Time-Trial
  • 8th: Hingene-Bornem
  • 36th: Molenbeek-Wersbeek
  • 67th: Stage 2, Tour of Britain Women
  • 24th: Stage 1, Tour of Britain Women

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 1st: 2023, 2024

Noemi Rüegg (Switzerland)

It’s been a tough year for Noemi Rüegg, who fought back from injury sustained crashing out of the Vuelta while in the red jersey, but she scored multiple top tens over the opening three stages on home roads in Switzerland at the Tour de France Femmes. She loves hillys races and has one of the best kicks in the game. She has a strong team here with TT World Champion Marlen Reusser and could take inspiration from the success of EF Education-EasyPost teammate Magdeleine Vallieres last year.

  • Read more: ‘I found my place at EF’: Noemi Rüegg Q&A

Road victories this season

  • Stage 1, La Vuelta Femenina
  • GC, Women’s Tour Down Under
  • Stage 3, Women’s Tour Down Under

Last five results

  • 3rd: World Championship Mixed Relay Team Time-Trial
  • 17th: Tour de Gatineau
  • 9th: Classic Lorient Agglomération
  • 10th: Kreiz Breizh Elites Féminin
  • 4th: Vivi Zuricrit

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 11th: 2024

Elisa Longo Borghini (Italy)

34-year-old Elisa Longo Borghini had a slow start to the season by her standards, missing out on a victory in the big Classics, but she achieved a huge third place at the Tour de France Femmes and still won stages across the UAE Tour, Giro d’Italia and Tour de Suisse. One look at her palmarès showcases her abilities in one-day races of all kinds over the years, whether it be the Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix Femmes or Brabantse Pijl.

The multiple Italian national champion has never quite had the edge to secure higher than a bronze medal in the road race, coming third in 2020 and 2024. She did help the team to a gold medal in the mixed relay team time-trial at the World Championships last week though, and had an impressive showing in the individual time-trial to finish fourth.

Road victories this season

  • World Championship Mixed Relay Team Time-Trial
  • Italy National Championships, Road Race
  • Stage 2, Tour de Suisse Women
  • Stage 9, Giro d’Italia Women
  • Trofeo Oro in Euro
  • GC, UAE Tour Women
  • Stage 4, UAE Tour Women

Last five results

  • 1st: World Championship Mixed Relay Team Time-Trial
  • 4th: World Championship Elite Women Individual Time-Trial
  • 8th: Pointe du Raz Ladies Classic
  • 12th: Tout commence en Finistère Ladies Classic
  • 3rd overall: Tour de France Femmes

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 3rd: 2020, 2024

Marlen Reusser (Switzerland)

Marlen Reusser has one gold medal from these World Championships already, claiming victory in the individual time-trial by some margin. The Swiss rider isn’t only fierce against the clock but it certainly helps her with solo attacks.

She’s had a strong season leading up to this, going late for final day and overall victory at the Tour de Suisse and having an excellent Tour de France until she crashed on the final stage. Her best result in the road race came in 2023 where she finished fourth, but has been strong in hilly Classics this year, beating Demi Vollering in the sprint to win Dwars door Vlaanderen in April.

Road victories this season

  • World Championship Elite Women Individual Time-Trial
  • Chrono Féminin de Gatineau
  • Stage 4 ITT, Tour de France Femmes
  • GC, Tour de Suisse Women
  • Stage 5, Tour de Suisse Women
  • Stage 4 ITT, Tour de Suisse Women
  • Dwars door Vlaanderen

Last five results

  • 3rd: World Championship Mixed Relay Team Time-Trial
  • 1st: World Championship Elite Women Individual Time-Trial
  • 1st: Chrono Féminin de Gatineau
  • 14th overall: Tour de France Femmes
  • 109th: Stage 9, Tour de France Femmes

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 4th: 2023

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Poland)

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney has had a season to remember, collecting a plethora of podiums in the Classics before coming so close to overall victory at the Tour after a commanding victory on Mont Ventoux. She hasn’t raced since the final stage of the Tour, so her form is somewhat of a mystery, but she always tends to show up in big races. Her best Worlds result to date is a bronze medal in 2021.

Road victories this season

  • Stage 7, Tour de France Femmes

Last five results

  • 3rd: Stage 9, Tour de France Femmes
  • 3rd: Stage 8, Tour de France Femmes
  • 1st: Stage 7, Tour de France Femmes
  • 18th: Stage 6, Tour de France Femmes
  • 3rd: Stage 5, Tour de France Femmes

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 3rd: 2021

Others

24-year-old Puck Pieterse (Netherlands) has been flying. She won the mountains classification at the Tour de France Femmes after a Classics season in which she finished second at both Liège-Bastogne-Liège and La Flèche Wallonne and third at the Tour of Flanders. Franziska Koch (Germany) reigned victorious at Paris-Roubaix Femmes, doubled up in the National Championships and podiumed in the individual time-trial at the World Championships last week, it could be a step too far for her with the hills on offer, however nothing would be a surprise with the form she’s shown.

Keep an eye on Cédrine Kerbaol (France) too. She scored multiple top ten results across the Tour de France Femmes that resulted in sixth place overall and clocked fifth in the individual time-trial in Montreal.

entry.title: Waxed Cotton with Ronnie Romance
entry.content:
Join Ronnie Romance inside Halley Stevensons in Dundee, Scotland, to discover how waxed cotton is made and why this centuries-old fabric still has a place in modern outdoor clothing.

The story of waxed cotton begins at sea. In the early 15th century, Scottish herring fishermen began treating their sails with fish oils and grease to protect them from the elements. Worn pieces of sailcloth were later repurposed as capes, helping sailors withstand wind and sea spray.

Since 1864, Halley Stevensons has continued to develop this tradition in Dundee. Today, the process brings together generations of knowledge, industrial machinery and a surprising amount of human touch.

For Ronnie, that is part of the appeal. Waxed cotton is durable, repairable and made to change with use. Marks, creases and patina become part of the fabric, while the surface can be re-waxed to maintain its weather resistance over time.

Check out more at Amundsen.

entry.title: Korean Coasts Part II: A Bicycle Journey Through Identity & Landscape – Molly Sugar
entry.content:
Molly Sugar shares excerpts from her Korean Coasts zine, exploring identity, belonging, and landscape as a Korean adoptee. The second chapter of her bicycle journey through Korea follows two very different rides: a solo bike tour along Korea’s East Coast and a group ride around Jeju Island with friends.

Returning

I have only spent a tiny fraction of my life in South Korea. I was adopted and brought to the United States when I was three months old, and for much of my life Korea existed more as an idea than a place I truly knew. How do you make up for lost time?

The reality is that you probably can’t, and I have come to accept that. What I do know is that I want to spend more time in my motherland and soak up as much as I can whenever I am there. For me, bicycle touring is the perfect way to experience a place. It allows me to move slowly through the landscape, meet people, eat local food, and process what it means to be an adoptee returning to the country where I was born.

I have now returned to Korea three times, and each visit has marked a different chapter in my life.

My first trip back as an adult was in my early twenties. I visited with former college roommates, one of whom was teaching English in Korea. We stayed out too late at clubs and noraebangs 노래방 (karaoke), checked off tourist sites like the DMZ and the National Palace, and ate as much incredible Korean food as possible. It was a fun introduction, but I left feeling like there was still so much more to understand.

By my second visit, in my mid-thirties, I knew I wanted to experience Korea by bike. Cycling has shaped much of my life, and it felt like the most natural way to explore my connection to the country. In the fall of 2024, I rode from Seoul to Busan with two friends, including a fellow Korean adoptee. The journey changed me. It deepened my connection to Korea and showed me how powerful a bicycle can be as a tool for exploration, reflection, and belonging. You can read more about that experience in Seoul to Busan: Part One. As soon as the trip ended, I knew I wanted to return.

For this third visit, I wanted something different. I wanted to experience Korea both alone and in community. I wanted to see new landscapes, eat new foods, and meet people in different corners of the country. So I chose two very different rides: a solo journey along Korea’s East Coast and a group ride around Jeju Island with friends.

The two experiences could not have been more different, yet both felt necessary. The solitude of the East Coast gave me space to reflect, while Jeju brought connection, laughter, and shared memories. Together, they created a trip that filled my heart in ways I did not expect.

This zine is a reflection on both journeys. It is part practical guide for anyone interested in bicycle touring in Korea and part personal exploration of what it means to return to a homeland as an adoptee. It is about bikes, but it is also about much more than bikes. It is about the ways identity and landscape become intertwined, and how moving through a place by bike can create space to heal, reconnect, and better understand where you come from.

East Coast

Korea’s East Coast Bike Route is a stunning coastal journey stretching roughly 300 miles between the northern border region near the DMZ and the city of Ulsan in the south.

Along the way, riders are treated to dramatic ocean views, quiet fishing villages, fresh seafood, and some of the most beautiful stretches of coastline in the country. Compared to Korea’s inland cycling routes, the East Coast is hillier and requires sharing more roads with cars, but the scenery makes every climb worthwhile.

The route is typically ridden northbound to take advantage of prevailing winds, but I rode it southbound and never felt like the wind was working against me. To reach the coast, I took an express bus from Seoul to Sokcho, where it was easy to store my bike underneath the bus. After spending the night in Sokcho, I rode north to the entrance of the Unification Observatory and then returned to town. This is the northernmost point you can reach by bike, as access to the actual observatory near the DMZ requires additional transportation by bus.

That northernmost section ended up being one of my favorite sections of the entire trip. The route felt surprisingly remote, winding through farmland and stretches of overgrown bike path. It was quiet in a way that I had not expected, and it gave me time to settle into the rhythm of traveling alone.

Most of the route passes through small beach communities, with cities like Gangneung and Donghae appearing every other day. Unlike the highly isolated and mostly car-free Cross-Country Path, the East Coast route frequently shares roads with local traffic. That said, I was pleasantly surprised by how many dedicated bike paths followed the shoreline. Some of my favorite stretches hugged the ocean for miles, offering uninterrupted views of the sea.

I ended my ride in Pohang, where it was easy to catch a bus to Busan. The bus system is incredibly convenient and offers several drop off locations throughout the city. Locals told me that the section between Pohang and Busan tends to be the busiest and least enjoyable part of the route due to heavier traffic, so I decided to skip it entirely without any regrets.

I rode the East Coast in late October, and the conditions could not have been better. After delaying my departure a few days to avoid heavy rain, I was rewarded with cool temperatures, clear skies, and comfortable riding weather. Spring and fall are generally the best seasons for cycling in Korea. Summer brings crowds to the beaches, while winter can be quite cold and windy along the coast.

If you love ocean views, colorful fishing harbors, seaside bike paths, fresh seafood, and small towns that seem untouched by time, the East Coast route is hard to beat. Along the way you’ll pass giant king crab statues, traditional wooden pavilions overlooking the sea, picturesque lighthouses, trendy surf shacks, and dramatic rocky shorelines. Just be prepared for the constant rhythm of the coast: up a hill, down a hill, and then right back up another one. The views are worth every pedal stroke.

Jeju Island

The Jeju Fantasy Bicycle Path truly lives up to its name. Circling the entire island for roughly 150 miles, the route offers stunning coastal views, volcanic landscapes, and some of the most scenic riding in Korea.

Compared to the East Coast and the inland Cross-Country Path, Jeju is generally flatter, with gentle rolling hills that make it one of the most approachable long distance bike routes in the country. Known as the Hawaii of Korea, Jeju is South Korea’s premier island getaway. Its mild climate, dramatic volcanic terrain, waterfalls, lava caves, and unique cultural traditions attract visitors from across the country and around the world. Because of its popularity, Jeju was also the busiest cycling route I rode in Korea.

After spending days riding solo along the East Coast, arriving in Jeju felt like stepping into a completely different experience. Instead of long stretches of solitude, I was riding with friends and surrounded by people. We saw more cyclists here than anywhere else, including several solo women travelers, which was especially exciting since I was the only solo woman cyclist on the East Coast.

What made Jeju special for me was not just the riding, but the opportunity to share it with friends. As much as I value solo travel, there was something refreshing about experiencing Korea in community. We spent our days riding the coastline and our evenings exploring together, visiting places like the Haenyeo Museum, learning about Jeju’s famous women divers, and even making a stop at the quirky Sex Museum. Many of Jeju’s meals are designed to be shared family style, so having friends along also meant I could enjoy dishes that would have been difficult to order alone.

While there are a few stretches of dedicated bike path, most of the route follows local roads shared with cars. Fortunately, drivers were generally patient and respectful, and I never felt uncomfortable riding alongside traffic. The eastern side of the island offers some quieter and more remote sections, which ended up being my favorite parts of the route.

We rode the island in the recommended counterclockwise direction, keeping the ocean on our right and taking advantage of the prevailing winds. To get there, we flew from Busan to Jeju and later from Jeju to Seoul. Flights take about an hour and are relatively affordable. Since we rented bikes on the island, we did not have to worry about flying with our own bikes, which made travel much simpler.

We rode Jeju in early November and were treated to mostly sunny skies and temperatures in the mid 60s. We did have one day of relentless rain and headwinds, which made me grateful it was the exception rather than the rule. While Jeju stays slightly warmer than the mainland, summers can be extremely humid and bring monsoon rains. Spring and fall are generally the best times to ride. Because the route is relatively flat, the island’s famous coastal winds are often the biggest challenge.

If you love beautiful coastlines, matriarchal cultural history, waterfalls, lava caves, and vibrant seaside towns, Jeju is hard to beat. Along the way you’ll pass sculptures honoring the Haenyeo women divers, wind farms, citrus farms, endless rows of drying squid, black volcanic cliffs, and countless ocean views. It is a route that feels both relaxed and adventurous, and one that is best enjoyed at a pace slow enough to take it all in.

Alone & Together

Before this trip, I had never bike toured alone for multiple days, let alone in another country. The idea of spending seven days riding solo along Korea’s East Coast felt both exciting and slightly intimidating.

As a Korean adoptee returning to my motherland, there was also an emotional side to traveling alone. Every day brought new experiences, unfamiliar places, and moments that stirred up feelings I wasn’t always expecting. Some days I felt deeply connected to Korea. Other days I felt like an outsider looking in.

There is something powerful about moving through the landscape of your birth country under your own power. Unlike visiting cities or checking off tourist attractions, cycling allows you to experience the spaces in between. The small towns, the farms, the roadside restaurants, and the everyday moments that most visitors pass by. Riding gave me the time and space to connect with Korea at a slower pace and reflect on my relationship to a place that feels both familiar and unfamiliar at the same time.

Traveling alone also meant there was nowhere to hide from my thoughts. Some days that felt challenging. Other days it felt like a gift. The long stretches of coastline, the rhythm of pedaling, and the quiet moments at the end of the day created space to process emotions that often get drowned out by the busyness of everyday life.

Then came Jeju.

After a week of solitude, arriving on Jeju Island with friends felt like stepping into a different version of the same journey. The landscapes were beautiful, but what stood out most was the sense of connection. Instead of spending my days alone with my thoughts, I spent them sharing meals, conversations, and experiences with people who understood why this trip mattered.

My friend Mai-li is also a Korean adoptee, and we had ridden Korea’s Cross-Country Path together the year before. My friend Sara’s mom is a Korean adoptee, and this was Sara’s first trip to Korea. In different ways, all three of us were navigating questions of identity, belonging, and what it meant to be in Korea.

We talked openly about the strange experience of feeling Korean but not fully Korean. Of being connected to a place while also feeling disconnected from it. Of wanting to learn more about our histories while trying to stay present and appreciate the experience in front of us. These conversations often happened while riding side by side, over shared meals, or during quiet moments at the end of the day.

The East Coast and Jeju offered two very different experiences, but I came to realize that I needed both. The solo ride gave me space for reflection, while Jeju reminded me of the importance of community. One helped me listen inward. The other helped me feel understood.
As adoptees, so much of our journey can feel solitary. This trip reminded me that it doesn’t always have to be. Sometimes the most meaningful part of returning is having people beside you who understand the questions you’re carrying, even if none of you have the answers.

Closing Reflections

One of my favorite moments on the East Coast happened after a particularly steep climb. Tired and grinding my way uphill, I finally reached the top and was rewarded with my favorite part of cycling: the descent.

As I flew down the steepest hill of the entire trip, I spotted a group of older women, ajummas, gathered at the bottom. As I passed, they started cheering and clapping for me. It was a small, unexpected moment, but one that has stayed with me long after the trip ended.
At that exact moment, I was listening to “Little Balcony” by Hyukoh and Sunset Rollercoaster:

You’re gone
Forever young
Eternal sun
Go have some fun
Don’t get me wrong
I love you so much
I’m glad you stop
Your endless run

The lyrics almost sound like a gentle voice saying: “You don’t have to keep running. You’re here. Enjoy this moment.” Something about the music, the cheering strangers, and the feeling of flying down that hill came together in a way that felt impossible to recreate. It was one of those fleeting travel moments that becomes larger in memory than it seemed at the time.

Riding alone on the East Coast and with friends on Jeju Island reminded me that I needed both experiences to fully embrace this return to Korea. The East Coast gave me space for solitude and reflection. Jeju brought connection, laughter, and community. Together, they created a journey that felt complete.

As adoptees, we often talk about searching for connection, belonging, or pieces of ourselves. Sometimes that search looks dramatic, but more often it happens in small moments: eating convenience store ramyeon after a long day of riding, watching the ocean waves from a harbor, reflecting on a funny conversation with a friend, or being cheered on by a group of ajummas at the bottom of a hill. Those moments became just as meaningful as the miles themselves.

I have only spent a small fraction of my life in Korea, but each visit deepens my connection to the place in ways I never expect. I know I can never make up for lost time, but I hope to keep returning. To discover more, learn more, and continue building my relationship with my motherland, one bike trip at a time.

If this zine resonated with you, consider supporting BIPOC Adoptees, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to creating safe, inclusive spaces for adoptees of color. Their mission is to uplift BIPOC adoptees through community, storytelling, education, and care, while challenging the systemic erasure and neglect adoptees often experience.

The post Korean Coasts Part II: A Bicycle Journey Through Identity & Landscape appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Norco adidas Race Division Teases Unreleased Frame and Shoes Ahead of Whistler World Cup
entry.content:
This weekend, the World Cup is heading to the iconic destination of Whistler, British Columbia, Canada. The legendary 1199 trail, featuring big jumps, steep chutes, and hectic rock gardens, will be used as the World Cup DH track for the first time. Whistler also happens to be in Norco’s backyard, so this is technically the Norco adidas Race Division’s home race. To mark the occasion, the team is going all in with custom-painted frames and a new race kit.

The Norco adidas Race Division (NaRD) consists of Gracey Hemstreet, Bodhi Kuhn, Danny Hart, and Lina Frener, and is coached by the GOAT, Greg Minnaar. The Norco team riders will be attacking the rough and unrelenting 1199 track in search of gold on bikes custom-painted with the “gold treatment”. According to Norco, “The bikes are layered with a deep colour flake, contrasted between violet, ‘frozen lemon’, and ivory, with gold flakes catching the light in the sun. An extra detail is tucked under the shock: a special call-out to each team member who contributed to racing this year.”

Bike Check

  • Frame: Norco Team DH
  • Fork: Fox 40 Factory
  • Shock: Fox DHX2 Factory
  • Drivetrain: Shimano Saint M820
  • Brakes: Shimano XTR M9200
  • Rims: Crankbrothers Synthesis DH
  • Hubs: Chris King
  • Stem & Handlebar: Raceface Atlas
  • Saddle: SDG I-Fly 2.0
  • Pedals: Crankbrothers Mallet DH

While the paint jobs certainly look pretty cool, perhaps the most interesting thing we noticed is the team’s DH frames. These are very clearly not the Torrent DH frame the brand launched earlier this summer. That’s obviously not a Horst-link suspension layout, and the difference in frame shape, along with the addition of an idler, points to a completely new DH platform. In fact, Norco hasn’t been keeping this unreleased bike much of a secret; it was just featured in NaRD’s “All Hands on Deck” video that came out a couple of days ago (see below). It seems the Norco team has been testing it most of the season and will be racing it again this weekend.

Matching Kits and Adidas Shoes?

Additionally, the NaRD team is getting new race kits that match their custom frame paint jobs. These new kits also strongly emphasize the classic adidas 3-stripe logo, with stripes that extend down the arms and legs all the way to the shoes. Yes, the shoes.

The NaRD team appears to be showing off some unreleased adidas mountain bike shoes, the same shoes that adidas has been teasing recently on its social media channels (see below). With dual BOA dials, those definitely look like MTB shoes, although the prominent 3-stripe branding and small 5-10 logo are a step in a different direction for the brand.

Clearly, neither the NaRD team nor adidas is intent on keeping these new shoes completely under wraps, but these pictures are really the only images we’ve seen of them thus far. We’re looking forward to learning more about them, and we’ll share that info when we do. In the meantime, be sure to tune in to the World Cup action this weekend. It’s sure to be an exciting time for all the racers in Whistler taking on 1199.

entry.title: Assos Drops New Equipe R Hydra Women’s and Mille GTS Sturmprinz Rain Jackets for Fall/Winter
entry.content:
With the arrival of fall and winter on the horizon, there’s no shortage of new cycling apparel and outerwear hitting the market right now. Assos of Switzerland recently added two new rain jackets to the mix, both of which are claimed to be “engineered for the demands of riding in the wettest conditions.” Developed with input from EF Pro Cycling’s riders, these new jackets have been designed to provide “serious waterproof protection with breathability, thermoregulation, and unrestricted movement.”

The new Mille GTS Sturmprinz Rain Jacket is an evolution of the original with an updated fit and modern materials for training or racing in the harshest conditions. With the new Equipe R Hydra Women’s Rain Jacket, Assos says it did not just adapt a male jacket (aka “shrink it and pink it”) for female cyclists. Instead, it started from scratch with a women’s-specific approach to create a high-performance rain jacket for female cyclists. Let’s check them out.

Equipe R Hydra Women’s Rain Jacket S11

Assos says women’s race equipment is often just an adaptation of products originally designed for male riders. Different colors, a smaller size run, and slight modifications to fit are sometimes all that separate men’s and women’s apparel. When designing the new Equipe R Women’s rain Jacket, the brand says that it took a different approach. According to Assos, this jacket is a purpose-built piece of race equipment that was developed around the riding position, ergonomics, and performance demands of female cyclists.

“The focus was on creating a race rain jacket that genuinely works with the female body and riding position,” says Elisabetta Borghin, Head of Women’s Product Development at ASSOS. “We worked closely with female pro riders throughout the development, using their feedback from training and racing to refine the fit, stretch, protection, and breathability.”

According to Assos, this female-first approach results in a jacket that provides an aerodynamic race fit that moves with the rider. At the same time, the lightweight waterproof shell keeps rain out and allows heat and moisture to escape, helping to regulate body temperature while training or racing in challenging conditions. Assos gives it a recommended temperature range of +4° / >+21°C.

Assos says its Hydra 3L softshell provides “complete stormproof protection with impossible breathability (50900 g/m²/24h) and a low-volume construction that packs down to the size of an accessory for pocket storage.” Taped seams, an ECO DWR treatment, and coated panels of highly elastic AVANTGARDE at the wrist openings and hem seal out moisture even further. All of the materials are OEKO-Tex certified and PFAS-free.

The Equipe R Hydra Women’s Rain Jacket features a two-way zip, allowing ventilation from the top or bottom. It also features reflective details to add visibility in low-light conditions that are common during the shorter days of the shoulder seasons, or riding when it’s overcast or rainy. The Equipe R Women’s Rain Jacket comes in six sizes, XS to 2XL, and the Kosimo Granit colorway only. It retails for £280 / €330 / $370.00.

Mille GTS Sturmprinz Rain Jacket S11

This new rain jacket builds on the legacy of the original Sturmprinz and moves it into Assos’s GTS collection. Constructed with the brand’s latest waterproof materials and an updated, performance fit, the GTS Mille Sturmprinz is intended to be adaptable to changing temperatures, weather conditions, and riding intensity. It has a claimed temperature range of -8° / +20°C.

The Mille GTS Sturmprinz is made with Assos’ ATLANTIS 3L hardshell fabric with a claimed breathability rating of 42,900 g/m²/24h. That “impossible breathability” is also combined with complete protection from water and wind across the front panel, shoulders, sides, and leading edge of the sleeves. The rear-facing panels on the body and sleeves utilize a CORE Light softshell fabric; all of the seams are taped, and the wrist cuffs and hem employ a coated elastic AVANTGARDE material, sealing out the elements completely.

That said, Assos included airVents on the upper back, a smart ventilation system they say “opens to expel heat in an upright climbing position.” The two-way zipper allows riders to vent from the bottom while maintaining full rain protection for the upper torso, neck, and shoulders. The Mille GTS Sturmprinz Rain Jacket comes in Fanatic Silver only and in seven sizes, XS to 3XL. It has a retail price of £410.00 / €490.00 / $585.00.

Availability

Assos of Switzerland’s latest Equipe R Hydra Women’s and Mille GTS Sturmprinz Rain Jackets are available now. Head to the Assos website to learn more about them and the rest of the brand’s extensive lineup of cycling apparel for men and women.

assos.com

entry.title: MVC Group Acquires Tailfin
entry.content:
The world of touring and bikepacking races has gotten a lot easier since Tailfin entered the market in 2017. With its smart rack and bag designs, just about any bike can be taken out on races, overnighters, or trips. We spoke with founder and CEO Nick Broadbent earlier this week when he told us that he’d sold a majority stake in the company to MVC Group, which was looking to broaden its portfolio…

MVC also owns Castelli and Sportful and has a presence in 75 countries through 10 subsidiaries. This acquisition will expand Tailfin’s global presence and streamline the company’s workflow.

Tailfin’s Founder, Nick Broadbent, and the entire management team we have grown to know over the years will continue to lead the company while retaining a minority stake. This keeps the soul of the company intact, ensuring its fortification of the Tailfin brand identity while offering support through a steadily growing community.

Read the full press release below:

MVC Group, a group specializing in technical apparel for cycling and outdoor sports, announces the acquisition of Tailfin, the global leader in the premium technical bikepacking segment.

Founded in Bristol in 2017 by Nick Broadbent – CEO, mechanical engineer and product designer – Tailfin has rapidly established itself as a leading international name in premium bikepacking bags, racks and accessories, combining design and performance with a strong focus on innovation. The company has developed proprietary technologies entirely in-house, protected by more than 20 granted and pending patents, building a leading position based on engineering excellence, materials research and rigorous product development and validation processes.

Over the past five years, Tailfin has achieved average annual growth of approximately 50%, reaching almost €10 million in revenues in 2025 across global markets. More than half of its revenues were generated in the US, UK and Germany, as the company progressively expanded its international presence. This growth will now be further supported by MVC Group’s commercial and industrial capabilities, backed by the Group’s presence in 75 countries through 10 subsidiaries.

Tailfin’s Founder and management team will continue to lead the company while retaining a minority stake, ensuring strategic continuity and preserving the innovation capabilities that have driven its growth and built a strong brand identity, now also supported by a steadily growing community.

The acquisition represents a significant acceleration of MVC Group’s development strategy, expanding its cycling offering with a brand whose positioning around excellence is highly aligned with and complementary to the technical apparel of Castelli and Sportful.

At the same time, MVC Group is acquiring a valuable pool of technological expertise, design capabilities and intellectual property that can also support the development of new solutions for triathlon and outdoor sports, where MVC Group operates with Zoot and Karpos respectively.

The acquisition announced today also has a positive impact on the development path outlined in MVC Group’s three-year Industrial Plan, which targeted €150 million in revenues by 2028. In light of the expanded Group perimeter and the growth opportunities generated by industrial and commercial synergies, MVC Group expects to revise its development targets upwards, while maintaining a solid financial structure consistent with its planned investments.

Emilio Foà, CEO of MVC Group, said: “The most valuable acquisitions are those that strengthen an organisation’s capabilities. With Tailfin, we are not simply adding a new product category: we are integrating a leading brand whose positioning around excellence and strong focus on innovation are fully aligned with our own brands, while also being complementary to their offering. We are also integrating a strategic asset: the company’s distinctive technological expertise and extensive intellectual property, which could generate product innovation across the different disciplines in which we operate, from cycling and triathlon to outdoor sports. We are delighted to welcome Nick and the entire team, and look forward to working together to unlock Tailfin’s significant potential for further international growth and to embark on a new phase of shared development.”

Nick Broadbent, Founder and CEO of Tailfin, commented: “Since Tailfin was founded, we have invested heavily in innovation to develop products that set the standard within the rapidly growing category of bikepacking and adventure cycling. Joining MVC Group will allow us to accelerate this journey further, leveraging the Group’s industrial strength and international presence, while preserving the identity, autonomy and innovation culture that have made Tailfin so successful.”

For MVC Group, this is the fourth transaction completed in less than a year, following the launch of its tenth international subsidiary in the UK last July; the acquisition of Wolvenberg in February, which led to the creation of MVC Benelux; and the transaction carried out through Zoot, the California-based triathlon apparel and accessories brand, which acquired its European distributor last October, creating Zoot Europe.

See more at Tailfin.

entry.title: The Road Logic Returns as the Tom Ritchey Signature Edition
entry.content:
Ritchey just announced the return of the Road Logic with a Signature Edition, offering a riding experience steeped in more than 50 years of life experiences, framebuilding heritage, innovation, and exploration…

It’s a legacy that traces back to the 1970s, when Tom Ritchey built his first road frame in his parents’ garage in northern California. Since then, Tom has continued to explore, experience, and innovate in ways that define the craft, and the Road Logic Signature Edition is the result of that expanding legacy: his prodigious experience with steel and mastery of the subtleties and details gleaned from his tenure in the art of creating bicycles.

Road Logic Tom Ritchey Signature Edition Quick Hits

  • Sizes: 49, 51, 53, 55, 57, 59cm
  • Heat-treated, triple-butted Ritchey Logic tubeset
  • TIG-welded
  • Ritchey full carbon fork
  • 700x30c tire clearance (depending on tire/rim manufacturer)
  • Headset: WCS drop in 1-1/8” (included)
  • Weight: 1.77kg (55cm – frame-only)
  • Color: Ritchey Classic Red
  • Price:
    • $1,759.00
    • €1,699.00
    • £1479.00

The beauty of its classic lines unites with modern building techniques and proven materials to deliver a contemporary bicycle that’s sufficiently comfortable for long days in the saddle, nimble and stiff enough to win the sprint for that sign, and adequately adaptable to endure roads that might lack proper pavement. Bearing Tom Ritchey’s signature on the top tube, it’s a subtle reminder that this frame is a direct expression of his lifelong dedication to steel and ride quality.

A true modern classic, the Road Logic Signature Edition uses a heat-treated and triple-butted Ritchey Logic tubeset that was designed by Tom, and it features aggressively short-butted sections optimized for TIG welding that save weight and improve ride quality. Ritchey’s proprietary forged-and-machined integrated head tube uses standard drop-in bearings and saves 80 grams over a standard head tube design.

Wrapped in Ritchey Classic Red paint, the Road Logic Signature Edition also features a Ritchey Carbon Fork and spacing for up to 30c tires to deliver a lifetime of enjoyable pedal turns.

entry.title: Bikepacking in Europe: Where to ride, how to pack and how to take it even further
entry.content:
Cyclist
Bikepacking in Europe: Where to ride, how to pack and how to take it even further

What Dan Burden first described as ‘bikepacking’ in a 1973 article in National Geographic would nowadays be called cycle-touring: he rode from Alaska to Southern Mexico over a year on a bike equipped with panniers carrying more than 20kg of luggage. The term bikepacking has come to describe a more aerodynamic and lightweight setup, although its widespread use sometimes covers anything from leisurely adventures to ultra-endurance racing.

Europe is particularly well suited to all forms of bikepacking adventures thanks to its relatively dense population, temperate climate and many small roads.

If you’re looking for your next adventure, here are three excellent European destinations to keep on your radar along with some packing tips, plus suggestions for those wanting to take things a step further into ultra-endurance events.

Three European destinations for bikepacking

Ireland’s Atlantic Coast

The Wild Atlantic Way runs along Ireland’s western coast from Muff in County Donegal to Kinsale in County Cork. It covers around 2,500km with 26,000m of elevation, providing enough terrain for a trip of several weeks, but individual sections can just as easily form the basis of a shorter bikepacking adventure.

The route was originally signposted in 2014 as a tourism route for drivers, taking visitors onto small scenic roads along the Atlantic coast. Riders who prefer to be away from motorised traffic as often as possible might be better off following Eurovelo 1 signs, which lead to nearby cycle paths and greenways.

The scenery changes considerably as the route progresses. County Mayo’s peat bogs and dark green hills have something of the character of Scotland, while further south, the craggy coastline offers a radically different landscape. In fact, I had to look twice at some pictures to differentiate between County Kerry and the South African coast.

Getting there is relatively simple. Trains connect Dublin with Derry/Londonderry and Cork, putting riders within reach of the northern and southern ends of the route.

There are plenty of B&Bs along the route, as well as campsites. Wild camping is tolerated in some remote areas, and it is often possible to find a friendly landowner willing to let you pitch a tent for the night.

  • Best time of year to go: late spring to early autumn. Avoiding the height of midge season (July and August) is advisable if camping.

Andalusia, Spain

The Andalusia region has many of the qualities that have made Girona a popular cycling destination, such as good roads and an established cycling culture, while also offering considerably more mountainous terrain.

It is not difficult to see why professional riders such as Jonas Vingegaard enjoy the region for winter training. The mild climate allows for substantial mileage during the cooler months, while the near-empty mountain roads provide a great playground for keen climbers. 

For a bikepacker, Málaga makes a convenient starting point. From there, riders can head towards Seville, Granada and Córdoba, linking up major historic cities with white villages that pepper the landscape, enjoying breathtaking views and occasional dips in reservoirs on the way.

Andalusia has many affordable guesthouses to offer, but few quiet campsites suitable for tents and wild camping is expressly prohibited, so the only option for a night under the stars is to set up a stealth bivvy.

  • Best time of year to go: March to June and late September to December. Summer is best avoided as temperatures can become extremely high, especially inland.

The Black Forest, Germany

The Black Forest in southwest Germany is particularly suited to gravel bikepacking. The region has an extensive network of small paved roads and well-maintained forest tracks, allowing riders to construct routes that combine both surfaces without spending much time on major roads.

It offers a useful combination of quiet riding, relatively straightforward logistics and enough climbing to make the route interesting. 

Freiburg im Breisgau is an easy starting point for a loop of 800km or more, taking in forest roads, local peaks and towns such as Baden-Baden, where hot springs feed fountains and spill from pipes and gutters.

German campsites often charge around €30 a night, even for riders carrying nothing more than a small tent. Forest shelters, known as Schutzhütten, where overnight stays are tolerated, can provide a more scenic alternative. Guesthouses are mostly cyclist-friendly and often cost only a little more than campsites. 

  • Best time of year to go: Spring or autumn. Summer often gets uncomfortably warm, and swarms of horseflies can make extended periods in the forest less appealing.

How can I pack efficiently without sacrificing the essentials?

Wherever you choose to go bikepacking, you will have to give careful consideration to your packing list. There is no shortage of ready-made packing lists from bikepackers, specialist websites and manufacturers, but ultimately the right setup depends on the rider and will be refined through trial and error.

The questions to ask are: what are my non-negotiables for comfort? What temperature variations and rainfall am I expecting? Will I be camping?

Here are some guidelines to start putting a list together without carrying superfluous items.

Question the necessity of each item

Make a list based on the cyclist version of an overnight bag, then go through it again asking whether you need each item and what would happen if you left it at home. 

Then, ask yourself how much of each item you need. If you are travelling for a week, you won’t go through an entire bar of soap, so cut it in half. 

Then, do a short test trip over a weekend. If an item comes home without having been used, consider striking off the list. A repair kit and first-aid bag are exceptions to this rule.

On the other hand, a rider needs to know their ‘non-negotiables’. For example, I am a minimalist bikepacker able to carry a total of 5kg including camping gear, but I always pack at least two pairs of gloves and four pairs of socks wherever I may go because I have poor circulation in my extremities.

If there is a particular part of your body, daily routine or sleeping routine that is disproportionately affected in tough environments, it is worth carrying what you need to deal with it.

The triple-two rule for compact packing

Packing is ultimately a compromise between weight and comfort, especially for those without a big budget. For space-efficient packing, I follow what I call the triple-two rule.

First, as far as possible, make sure that no two things share a purpose. If I need something to eat with, I will normally choose either a fork or a spoon rather than carrying both, having found that I usually end up with a favourite implement a couple of days in.

Second, make sure that every item serves at least two purposes. A thin scarf can double as a fast-drying towel; a cold-processed bar of soap can be used for personal hygiene and laundry.

Third, make sure that containers hold at least two things if they are not full – a pair of brake pads just about fits in the little box that contains my spare cleats.

A few must-haves

Here are a few items you should think twice about leaving behind:

  • An adventure-ready repair kit containing what you would take on a day ride as well as an extra tube, a tiny bottle of lube or drip wax, and some tape or zip-ties. For a longer or more remote trip, consider carrying a couple of spare spokes. Even if you do not know how to fit them yourself, having the correct spokes available means that the first bike shop you reach can fit them without having to order in the right size.
  • A first-aid kit and an emergency blanket for remote, cold or hot trips.
  • Spare shoes. Even trips with very little walking planned warrant a spare pair of shoes to let your feet air out. Sliders are particularly useful because they are light, can be strapped to the outside of a bag and can be worn with socks on chilly evenings.
  • A set of clothes that stays clean and dry no matter what. Camping in the rain is only made more miserable by the prospect of getting into dirty clothes at night. One shirt and a pair of shorts that took a lot of effort to keep smelling nice are sometimes a bikepacker’s only solace.

Some items fall into the ‘nice-to-have’ category. A Fiber Fix emergency replacement spoke is useful for a temporary repair without having to dismantle a cassette or rotor. I also use a Wippermann Connex chain link, which can be fitted and removed by hand. I regularly remove my chain, go and deep clean it in a sink, and fit it back on, all within a few minutes.

Ready for a bigger challenge?

Audax

Audaxes are non-competitive events (ie, without a finishers’ ranking) ranging from 200km to over 1,000km and where participants need to prove their presence at designated checkpoints via an app or in a more traditional way, by asking a local business to stamp a paper card. Up until a few years ago, audaxes were dominated by men over 50.

While you may still see the odd 20-year-old aluminium frame featuring strategically placed cardboard and duct tape in an attempt to improve its aerodynamics, audaxes have recently enjoyed a revival with the emergence of ultracycling. Their ranks have been widened by riders of all ages using this informal setting to build the experience required for ultra-endurance events.

For riders wanting to take the next step, there is now a broad range of ultra-endurance events in Europe. I asked ultracyclist and ultracycling coach Nathalie Baillon for recommendations. Baillon holds the Guinness World Record for the fastest women’s cycling crossing of Europe from Tarifa to the North Cape, and regularly finishes on the podium at ultra-endurance events.

Friendly ultras

For Baillon, Desertus Bikus and B-HARD Ultra Race stood out as good events for first timers.

  • Desertus Bikus (1,300km/13,000m elevation) has checkpoints located on gravel sections across Spain but allows riders to choose their own route between them. This gives the event a strong bikepacking character: route planning, navigation, food, sleep and mechanical decisions all form part of the challenge.
  • B-HARD Ultra Race (1,215km/16,000m elevation) in Bosnia and Herzegovina was designed to promote tourism and so that riders enjoy local sites and hospitality instead of zooming through landscapes to get to the finish line. It has a reputation for good organisation and a friendly atmosphere, while the route provides substantial climbing and varied terrain. 
  • The Wild West Country (750km/11,000m elevation) is my personal addition to Baillon’s list. While the top participants are competitive and the route through Devon and Cornwall is challenging, some less demanding transitional sections and fairly generous cutoffs make it a good event for beginners. Its much tougher big sister, The Perfidious Albion (1,600km/23,000m elevation), is still a niche event so the atmosphere is friendly, yet it seems like a good playing field for record-breaking attempts.

Competitive ultras

For riders looking for even more challenging rides and competitive fields, Baillon points to the Transcontinental Race on road and Badlands on gravel.

  • The Transcontinental Race (about 4,000km/40,000m elevation) has established itself as the holy grail of ultras. It has unforgiving cut-off times, strict rules, and combines extreme distance with self-supported racing, requiring riders to make decisions about routing, sleep, food and equipment while racing across Europe against a large pool of competitive athletes.
  • Badlands (about 800km/16,000m elevation) offers gravel riders a comparable level of commitment on a very different type of terrain, with remote sections and significant elevation through southern Spain.

Baillon also points to the Race Across Series of competitive events that offer a wide range of distances and features ‘living bases’ where participants can stop to rest and receive assistance, otherwise forbidden in ultra-racing. 

Time to hit the road 

Bikepacking is not necessarily a route towards ultra-endurance. It can simply be a way of travelling with little luggage and a lot of freedom. For riders who eventually decide they want to race across a country or continent, however, it provides a useful education.

The post Bikepacking in Europe: Where to ride, how to pack and how to take it even further appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Moots Has Redesigned the Routt for Modern Gravel
entry.content:
Steamboat Springs-based Moots, the Masters of Metal, has been building the Routt since 2013, and the all-new version, announced today, reflects how much gravel has changed since then…

More Routt More Rubber

The new Routt is our large-format gravel bike, designed around a 50 mm tire with clearance for up to 57 mm. Getting there meant reworking the frame around a new 3D-printed chainstay yoke, in-house machined UDH dropouts, and a redesigned Moots carbon gravel fork with fully integrated brake routing through our in-house titanium stem. It’s the next step for the Routt, built around where gravel is now.

Chassis Details

  • A 3D-printed chainstay yoke creates room for up to a 57mm tire while maintaining clearance for up to a 48T 1x chainring.
  • Redesigned Moots carbon gravel fork with a new D-shaped steerer allows fully integrated brake routing through our Moots Ti stem for a clean, integrated front end.
  • In-house machined UDH dropouts are designed and machined in Steamboat for current and future drivetrain compatibility.
  • Broader drivetrain options include compatibility with traditional gravel drivetrains or wide-range mullet setups, giving riders more flexibility in how they build the bike.

Routt Geometry

The above geometry chart is based around a 50 mm tire, with sizing from a 50 mm, which is specced with a 52 mm top tube, up through a 60 mm with a 60.5 mm top tube. Variable head tube and seat tube angles run across the sizing range with constant 43.7 cm chainstays.

Two Models of Routt

RSL is now offered as a premium frame upgrade rather than a separate model, giving riders one platform with two distinct tubing options.

Routt

Straight-gauge 3/2.5 titanium tubing gives the standard Routt the classic Moots ride: balanced, durable, and suited to long days and mixed terrain.

  • Straight-gauge 3/2.5 titanium
  • Balanced ride feel
  • Built for all-around gravel use

Routt RSL (available early 2027)

The RSL upgrade uses ride-tuned, double-butted titanium tubing to remove weight and sharpen the feel under power. It’s aimed at riders building toward a lighter, more race-focused setup.

  • Double-butted RSL titanium tubing
  • Lower frame weight
  • Quicker, more direct feel
  • Built with performance and weight savings in mind

See more of the new Routt at Moots.

The post Moots Has Redesigned the Routt for Modern Gravel appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: State Bicycle Co Rolls Out New 4130 All Road Flat Bar
entry.content:
State Bicycle Co took its 4130 All Road bike and changed the geometry to accommodate flat bars, resulting in the 4130 All Road Flat Bar ($899.99), and making for an entirely new chassis and stance…

The 4130 All Road Flat Bar looks more like a 90s MTB than it does an all-road bike. This new model blends the past with the best of modern components, offering UDH, hydraulic braking, and Microshift 10-speed shifting. A simple bike utilizing common standards and completely external cable routing for ease of maintenance, repair, and upgrade.

Designed for meandering riding both loaded and unloaded with taller stack and stable handling. The 4130 Flat Bar has 450 mm chainstays across the entire size range, and comes stock with 650b tires with clearance for up to a 2.4″ rubber. For those who prefer a larger wheel, 700 x 2.25″ clearance makes this a versatile bike for a wide range of riders. Speaking of range, the 11-46 tooth cassette delivers, paired with a 40t narrow/wide ring up front.

Best of all, the complete bikes start at just $899.00 USD, with a variety of upgrade options available.

Specs:

  • 650 x 2.1 Vittoria Tires
  • UDH Compatibility
  • Hydraulic Disc Brakes
  • Full Chrome Finish Kit
  • Color Options: Black Stone / Schoolyard Yellow / Mint Chocolate Chip
  • MSRP: $899.99 USD

entry.title: Castelli Launches Perfetto 4, Perfetto Pro, and Gabba Pro Jackets Made with Polartec AirCore
entry.content:
Yesterday, on the official first day of fall, Castelli introduced three new jackets for riding in the cool temperatures and/or inclement weather that lie ahead. Building on the success of the Perfetto RoS 3, the new Perfetto 4, Perfetto Pro, and Gabba Pro are the next generation of jackets to feature the revolutionary Polartec AirCore fabric. Introduced last year, AirCore was developed in partnership with Polartec and is exclusive to Castelli (and sister company Sportful).

Now, Castelli is incorporating this lightweight, breathable, windproof, and water-repellent fabric into three new jackets. The Perfetto 4 (men’s and women’s) adds more loft and insulation for everyday riders. The Perfetto Pro (men’s only) takes a more streamlined, race-ready approach. And the Gabba Pro (men’s only) introduces AirCore into the iconic, race-ready Gabba range. Let’s check them out.

Castelli Perfetto 4

With the 4th generation of the Perfetto, Castelli chose to split it into two distinct models: the Perfetto 4 and the racier Perfetto Pro. According to the brand, rider feedback suggested that the Perfetto RoS 3 was lighter and therefore less warm than previous versions. Taking this into account, they introduced a new 219g AirCore fabric to give the Perfetto 4 more loft and insulation, which gives it a recommended temperature range of 4-12°C / 39-53°F. 

That AirCore fabric is PFAS-free with a semi-air-permeable membrane, and it reportedly breathes so well that Castelli removed the zippered vents found on the previous version. The tailored fit includes a redesigned splash tail to protect against road spray, along with metal drainage holes in the rear pockets. The Perfetto’s recognizable shoulder taping has also been updated, with the transparent chameleon tape providing a similar but fresh look. 

  • Fit: Tailored
  • Weight: 286g (men’s), 239g (women’s)
  • Sizes: XS-3XL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s)
  • Colors: Black, Brilliant Orange, Steel Fade, and Twilight Blue (men’s) and Black, Hibiscus, and Twilight Blue (women’s)
  • Recommended Temp. Range: 4-12°C / 39-53°F
  • RRP €260 | $330 | £280

Castelli Perfetto Pro

The Pro version reimagines the Perfetto as a more streamlined, minimalist race piece with more of an emphasis on maximizing breathability and stretch. It’s made with a 150g AirCore fabric, “which delivers an optimal balance of breathability, stretch and protection for riders operating at higher speeds and sustained intensity.” Castelli says the Soudal Quick-Step team has been using it since the start of the season.

According to the brand, the Perfetto Pro’s lighter AirCore fabric has a temperature sweet spot of 6-14°C / 42-57°F, while fending off light showers and road spray. Transparent tape on the shoulder seams adds reinforcement and targeted rain protection without adding bulk. The two-way zipper allows you to dump heat on your terms, while the splash tail and floating pocket design have been refined from the Gabba R.

  • Fit: Race
  • Weight: 226g (men’s only)
  • Sizes: XS-3XL
  • Colors: Belgian Blue, Black, Electric Lime, and Shadow
  • Recommended Temp. Range: 6-14°C / 42-57°F
  • RRP €280 | $350 | £300

Castelli Gabba Pro

With the Gabba Pro, Castelli essentially took the same 150g AirCore fabric and body-hugging fit as the Perfetto Pro and made it into a short-sleeved jacket. As such, it looks nearly identical to the Perfetto Pro, but has short sleeves and only comes in Black or a Black Race Edition with pro racer-inspired logos. The Gabba Pro is only available online.

  • Fit: Race
  • Weight: 196g (men’s only)
  • Sizes: XS-3XL
  • Colors: Black and Black Race Edition
  • Recommended Temp. Range: 6-14°C / 42-57°F
  • RRP €260 | $320 | £230
  • Availability: Online exclusive

“It’s always an exciting moment introducing a new Gabba into the range, as it’s a jacket that revolutionized the cycling apparel market in the same way AirCore™ transformed how modern cyclists dress for colder conditions. This, and the Perfetto Pro, are jackets you want to wear when you need breathability, mobility, and a competitive edge, while the Perfetto 4 is everything you loved about our previous Perfettos, but taken to the next level. All three jackets provide excellent warmth, breathability, and protection against intermittent showers, but if torrential rain is forecast, we’d recommend the Gabba R for complete waterproof coverage.”

-Steve Smith, Castelli Global Brand Manager

Polartec AirCore

Here’s a quick refresher on Polartec AirCore. The AirCore fabric was co-developed by Castelli and Polartec. It is engineered from recycled polyester yarns with the goal of creating a tight membrane that blocks the elements but still allows air permeability. In the development process, breathability was prioritized over water-repellency. This is because they believe getting wet from sweat inside a jacket is just as problematic as getting wet from the rain.

According to Castelli, AirCore “was engineered to be both essentially windproof and waterproof.” It blocks the majority of wind, but lets a nearly imperceptible amount of air in — permeability is claimed at 0.7 cubic feet per minute. The hydrostatic pressure test score of 5,000 mm means that it is highly water-resistant — essentially waterproof — too. 

According to Castelli, “AirCore actively ventilates sweat away from riders’ bodies using the natural power of airflow, creating a microclimate that keeps the core stable and performance high, even during the most intense rides.”

In the cycling industry, Castelli and its sister brand Sportful have exclusive rights to the use of Polartec AirCore fabrics. We’re told that numerous other outdoor clothing brands will be utilizing AirCore technology and fabrics this winter.

Availability

The new Perfetto 4, Perfetto Pro, and Gabba Pro jackets made with Polartec AirCore fabrics are available now. Head to the Castelli website to learn more or find a dealer near you.

castelli-cycling.com
