entry.title: Paul’s 2026 Bespoked Dresden Reflection – Paul Kalifatidi & Stefan Haehnel
entry.content:
For our final piece of The Radavist’s 2026 Bespoked Dresden coverage, we’re handing the mic over to first-time attendee Paul Kalifatidi. Accompanying Paul’s first impressions and a selection of his photos are exquisite Bespoked booth photos by German photographer Stefan Haehnel. Read on for Paul’s musings and Stefan’s visual artistry…

I went to Bespoked with few expectations; those few being: is an event at the airport going to feel weird? And will there be a noticeable difference between this event and the only other bike show I’ve attended? I was pleasantly surprised by the answer to both.

Bespoked Dresden was held in the international airport, Flughafen Dresden, for the fourth year in a row. For me, it was fresh, as I had never been. The only other bike show, at least one that compared in scope to Bespoked, that I have been to has been the four years of the Made Bike Show in Portland, OR. The two venues could not have been starker in contrast.

This piece wasn’t meant to read like a comparison of the two events; it’s just that these are the only two comparable events I have been to.

Venue Differences

Made was held at Zidell Yards, a largely abandoned boatyard that the city has condemned. The floor is dirty, the light inside is nonexistent, and yet I love it. I know lots of people are looking forward to next year’s venue at the Portland Convention Center, but I’m going to miss the dingy, dark industrial setting at the boatyard. It has its charm, even if you might trip in a pothole while sweating out every pore of your body while trying to enjoy said charm.

Bespoke Dresden has the opposite venue: the second and third floor of a skylight-filled German airport.

I think most of my photos from the event were shot at ISOs below 800, a pleasant change. Photographing bikes was harder; navigating multiple escalators, stairs, or an elevator adds significant time. I only photographed 14 bikes at Bespoked while I shot 27 at Made. John had his workflow dialed in Dresden and shot more than he did at Made, which was crazy impressive. I really enjoyed the airy venue; it still had the industrial vibes I like, but in a clean, refined way.

Techno Culture

Another thing that I knew about going in but wasn’t sure what to think of was the displays. I once came across an Instagram Reel that explained why Germany gravitates towards electronic music, and I think it’s a rather fitting analogy for something that seems trivial: the displays at Bespoked.

In this video, the presenter explains that German society scores highly on uncertainty avoidance, the cultural preference for structure over chaos. Perhaps this is a symptom of the notoriously rigid societal expectations and German infrastructure, or the reason. There were two great examples of this on our train commutes in Germany. John got in trouble with the ticket lady for incorrectly stamping his train ticket, and a glass breaker intended for emergencies was captioned with “misuse will be punished.”

Anyways, back to the Instagram reel. The video explains that this rigorous adherence to structure is what allows the mind to unplug in the right setting. That is reflected in German EDM culture. The beat of German techno is monotonous, and the expectations for entering a German club are strict. Black clothing, stickers over camera lenses, and strict expectations regarding personal conduct actually facilitate interpersonal connection. By stripping much of the performance and synchronizing everyone’s brain waves to the same beat, personality is laid bare, and you somehow find a semblance of camaraderie with a room full of sweaty strangers.

But how does that connect to Bespoked?

Bespoked Booths as Canvases

Bespoked provides every exhibitor with a large wooden display and accompanying lighting. My concern was that the individuality and vision of every builder wouldn’t be on display. For example, at Made, every builder or booth is responsible for their display. Some are great. Some are not so great. That ends up having a huge effect on how showgoers interact with the booth and the bikes.

The most stunning bike might be on display in a pretty poorly curated display, and therefore, receive very little attention. Builders with a fine eye for design beyond bikes are rewarded, but novices are left shrouded in shadow. Bespoked fixed this issue. Every booth starts with the same canvas: a wooden board that is customized with peg boards and shelves. Integrated lighting becomes a constant, not a variable. By creating a strict outline and level playing field, ironically, the individuality of every builder flourished.

Now, the wares of every maker, be it bikes, bags, or components, were the display, not the booth itself. Take, for example, Jergen Gertze of Giawasa. It was his first show. The track bike he brought, Katana, was stunning. His display would not indicate that this was the first full-size bicycle that he had ever built, and I think that can only help new builders like him. This choice had the complete opposite effect that was anticipated.

Innovative Showcase

Seeing as we posted a rather controversial Dust Up on Europe being the new home of innovative bike design, I want to carefully and briefly touch on that. When I say brief, I mean brief. I’m going to give you one, maybe two, perhaps three paragraphs on the subject.

After walking around the venue for only 30 minutes, I told John just how different I thought the bikes were. There were certainly lots of funky bikes designed to be just that, contraptions for the sake of enjoyment at a bike show, but there were also innovative bikes meant to be just as functional as they were eye-catching.

The pervasive bike culture in the United States is that bikes are toys first and tools second. In Europe, bikes as playthings certainly exist, but so do thousands of unassuming and uninteresting, everyday bikes locked up outside a train station, even in a smaller East German city not known for its bike infrastructure.

Good luck finding that in the US. I’m not here to debate why this is or to throw shade at anything. I just want to say that this mindset seems to be reflected in the types of bikes that framebuilders are making. I don’t have statistics or facts to back this up, just my overall impression.

Sport Versus Transport

The bikes at American shows tend to be far more expensive and far more focused on hobbies: racing, mountain biking, gravel biking, that sort of thing. In this European show, it felt like there were more bikes meant to be ridden every day and were priced more appropriately for such a life.

There were more “commuter bikes” like cargo bikes compared to “play bikes” like gravel bikes at Bespoked than at any other bike show I had attended. I don’t think there is anything better or worse about this difference; it is merely an observation. This is, after all, a written impression of a European bike show by a young American journalist who doesn’t yet own a cargo bike.

When I came back from Germany, friends asked me if I had fun or got to see much of Dresden and Germany. The reality of these events is that just about every waking hour is spent commuting to and from the venue, taking photos, walking bikes between booths and photo spots, editing, writing, or engaging in the dinner pleasantries associated with the event.

European Impressions

Aside from the short bike ride I did aboard Petor’s “Room on the Broom” Drust or the one night of Technoclubbing, I did not get out much. And yet, I came back from Europe with a full heart. I met so many wonderful people at this show, and that alone made the short sleeps and long days worth it. I didn’t have to travel and see parts of the European continent that I haven’t in order to make this trip feel fulfilling.

Thank you to every single one of you who sent us an email, a DM, or a heartfelt hug at the event for being such a bright light.

I’m not quite sure how to wrap up this piece besides acknowledging that I don’t think it will be the last reflection I write about this event. I would love to have the opportunity to visit all of the Bespoked events, as I think they truly are something special.

Petor, and to all the others who help organize and put on these events, thank you for your work and dedication. To the builders and exhibitors, I can’t wait to see what the future has in store for you. Thank you, everyone.

Check out our hard work below…

The post Paul’s 2026 Bespoked Dresden Reflection appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: JF Frankel Comics: Major Taylor – JF Frankel
entry.content:
In the latest installment of JF Frankel’s comics, we have his conversation with long-time friend and cartoonist Frederick Noland. Noland recenlty published an illustrated history of Major Taylor and his accomplishments. JF draws a picture of the impetus and inspiration for Frederick’s new book. Check out the comic below…

About Frederick Nolan’s Major Taylor World’s Fastest Man

Marshall Walter “Major” Taylor was one of the greatest American athletes of the early 20th century, setting records in regional bike races as a teen and winning his first world championship by the age of twenty. But Taylor was born in 1878 in Indianapolis and came of age during the height of the Jim Crow era, facing racism at every turn.

Cartoonist Frederick Noland is a cyclist himself and in this epic 400 page graphic biography of America’s first Black world champion, he thrills in the records Taylor broke and the adoring public he found across North America, Europe, and Australia, all the while showing how the invention of the bicycle changed society. Yet Noland also documents how racism inflected Black life in the post Civil War era: cyclists would collude to injure Taylor, and he faced segregationist policies even in liberal cities such as San Francisco. And while Taylor found respite racing overseas, he soon found American-style racism exported internationally to sell tickets.

Noland pens a gorgeous, humane, graphic paean to Major Taylor, illustrating how the fastest man in America also had a deep well of integrity and fortitude not just to succeed, but to overcome the racist abuse he faced from fellow athletes and society at large. Major Taylor is a loving tribute to an exceptional American.

Get your copy of the Major Taylor book today!

entry.title: Bloomberg on Lauf’s VA Operations: A $5,000 Bike Shows Why It’s Hard to Build in America
entry.content:
For a journalistic deep dive into how the Trump Administration’s tariffs are affecting US manufacturing, check out this article in Bloomberg that focuses on Lauf Cycles‘ assembly factory in Harrisonburg, Virginia. Here’s an excerpt:

“President Donald Trump’s tariffs are supposed to bring manufacturing back to America. But a bicycle factory in Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains shows how the levies themselves often sabotage that goal.

Inside the Lauf Cycles plant in Harrisonburg, a half-dozen mechanics hover over ultra-light carbon fiber frames, threading chains through drivetrains, torquing down bolts and wrapping handlebars in tape. By assembling bikes here, in this former newspaper printing hall, the Icelandic company avoids tariffs the US slaps on imported bicycles — duties that run as high as 48.5%.”

“But nearly all the parts that go into a Lauf bike — including the company’s signature shock-absorbing fork — come from abroad. Each faces its own tariff. In most cases, there are no US-made replacements available. Last year, Lauf briefly paid levies above 170% on its frames and forks because they were made in China. The tariff on Chinese frames has since dropped to 41% — still steep.”

See more at Bloomberg.

The post Bloomberg on Lauf’s VA Operations: A $5,000 Bike Shows Why It’s Hard to Build in America appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Ornot Special Projects: Short Sleeve Micro Grid Jersey and Micro Climate Vest
entry.content:
Continuing in the pursuit of making limited-edition silhouettes from deadstock fabrics, Ornot just rolled out its long-awaited Micro Grid Jersey ($165) and a Micro Climate Vest ($158)…

 

Micro Grid Jersey

The Micro Grid Jersey is made in the USA from lightweight Polartec Power Grid, this short-sleeve jersey is designed to keep you cool down to the 50º range when paired with a lightweight jacket or vest, while the highly breathable fabric performs on its own up into the 80º range.

Typically, the brushed grid structure used in this jersey is associated with thermal clothing, but this version is light enough for summer temps. The small voids created by the grid, along with the fine knit, let air pass through. This keeps you cool when it’s hot. On the flip side, when you add a wind-blocking layer, those same air pockets keep you warm while wicking moisture away from your skin. It’s like magic (or just physics).

This jersey is made entirely from deadstock fabric and built right here in Oakland, California. Available in both men’s and women’s variants with a new, updated fit, this could be your only jersey, Ornot.

Specs:

  • Extremely wicking and breathable.
  • Anti-Microbial Treatment.
  • bluesign®-approved Polartec deadstock fabric.
  • Temperature range: 55-85 degrees, perfect for layering.
  • 3 rear pockets, YKK zipper, reflective details.
  • Sewn by hand in California.
  • MSRP: $165 USD

Micro Climate Vest

The Micro Climate Vest is Ornot’s ultimate choice for breathable warmth. Based on its award-winning Micro Climate Jacket, this vest features a flocked front and a lightweight grid fleece back for an ideal balance of insulation and breathability. For this season, Ornot brought back 3 rear pockets, added reflective details, and wrapped it up with a 2-way zipper.

Available in both men’s and women’s variants, you could call it a Gilet, Ornot. Made in Oakland, CA.

Specs:

  • 3 rear pockets.
  • Water-resistant and quick-drying due to patented thread treatment on the front panel.
  • 2-way YKK zipper for venting and pocket access.
  • 125 grams (size small) – Temp range: 40 – 67 degrees.
  • Reflective details on shoulder and back.
  • Breathable Polartec grid fleece on back and neck interior.
  • Sewn by hand in California.
  • Made using OEKO-TEX and bluesign®-approved fabric.
  • Men’s and Women’s Variants
  • MSRP: $158 USD

entry.title: Fairlight Secan 3.0 in Moorland Silver
entry.content:
UK brand Fairlight Cycles‘ new Secan 3.0 paint, Moorland Silver, is inspired by the silver hued grasses carpeting the moorlands surrounding Fairlight’s riding terrain. Moorland Silver is a metallic paint that comes in on the warmer spectrum, rather than the cooler side, with a lovely champagne warmth that comes through in low light. As with all Secan and Strael finish options, it is hand-sprayed and emery-clothed between every layer. The result is a premium, liquid finish with depth and shine.

Fairlight’s first batch has arrived this week, so if you’re interested, roll on over to Fairlight to see more.

entry.title: Castelli updates the Gabba and Perfetto with new Polartec AirCore fabric
entry.content:
Cyclist
Castelli updates the Gabba and Perfetto with new Polartec AirCore fabric

The Castelli Gabba has had a makeover, with its fourth generation switching from Gore-Tex Infinium fabric to Polartec AirCore. Now called the Gabba Pro, it’s joined by the new long sleeved Perfetto 4 and Perfetto Pro in using Polartec’s new fabric. 

Castelli worked with Polartec to develop AirCore, which it claims is not only water-repellent and windproof, but also lightweight, highly breathable and PFAS-free. 

Launching the new Gabba Pro, Castelli global brand manager, Steve Smith said, ‘It’s always an exciting moment introducing a new Gabba into the range as it’s a jacket that revolutionised the cycling apparel market in the same way AirCore transformed how modern cyclists dress for colder conditions.’

The Castelli Gabba Pro uses 150gsm AirCore fabric, which Smith says is tuned for riding at higher speeds and intensity. It has a close-to-body fit and short sleeves and is designed to be worn with arm warmers when it’s cool. As well as the all-black option, there’s a Race Edition, which comes complete with pro-style logos on the upper chest.

Castelli says that the Gabba Pro weighs 196g in an unspecified size. It’s available in men’s fit only, in sizes XS to 3XL and is priced at £230 / $320 / €260. For the moment, it’s only available via Castelli’s website.

Update to the Castelli Perfetto and the new Perfetto Pro

Castelli launched the Perfetto RoS 3 last year, the first use of this AirCore fabric worldwide.

But Smith says that customer feedback on the Perfetto RoS 3 was that they wanted more warmth, so in response the Perfetto 4, designed for everyday riders, uses a more insulated 219gsm version of AirCore.

Castelli says the Perfetto 4 is tailored for temperatures between 40C and 120C, with light showers a possibility. The contrasting shoulder taping that was a feature of the older Perfetto and the Gabba RoS is transparent on the new jackets. 

It has eliminated the venting zips, as it claims that the new jacket’s breathability is adequate without. There’s an updated tail to fend off road spray and metal drainage holes have returned to the pockets – a feature of the original Gabba when it was launched in 2013.   

The Perfetto 4 is available in men’s sizes from XS to 3XL and four colours and women’s sizes from XS to XL and three colours. Castelli claims a weight of 286g for the men’s and 239g for the women’s jacket. 

It’s priced at £280 / $330 / €260.

As with the Gabba, the Perfetto 4 Pro uses the original 150gsm AirCore. It’s cut differently to the Perfetto 4 too, with a closer, sleeker fit. It is available in men’s fit only, sizes XS to 3XL and again in four colours. It’s claimed to weigh 226g and is priced at £300 / $350 / €280.   

‘All three jackets provide excellent warmth, breathability and protection against intermittent showers but if torrential rain is forecast, we’d recommend the Gabba R for complete waterproof coverage,’ says Smith.

The three jackets aren’t the only Castelli products to use AirCore, with a raft of other jackets launched last year using the product, including the suitably named AirCore One and the Alpha 150, which uses an AirCore outer layer with a Polartec Alpha insulating layer underneath. The fabric also finds its way into the Polare bib tights and even the Estremo 2 shoe covers.

AirCore is made from recycled polyester, with a very tight weave to repel water but retain high breathability, so that riders don’t get drenched with sweat in place of rain. Polartec claims water vapour permeability of 25,000 g/m²/24h and that AirCore will support a hydrostatic head of 5,000mm. Castelli and Sportful have exclusive use of the fabric for cycling garments. 

The post Castelli updates the Gabba and Perfetto with new Polartec AirCore fabric appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: ‘I found my place at EF’: Noemi Rüegg Q&A
entry.content:
Cyclist
‘I found my place at EF’: Noemi Rüegg Q&A

How are you feeling about the upcoming World Championships?

I’m feeling good. Really excited. I’ve been looking forward to it for a long time, and I think we have a really strong Swiss team, so we have many cards to play. It’s gonna be an exciting race I think.

You’ve had the World Champion, Magdeleine Vallieres, on your team this past season. That must be quite inspiring. Does it make you dream about what’s possible?

Yeah, totally. I think last year’s Worlds showed that it’s a super-open race, and basically anyone can win. It’s very tactical, so you have to play it really smart because it’s a different race than any we do with our normal team. We have no radio, so it’s really hard to keep it under control. Last year showed that anything can happen. And it was so nice to see Mags winning. She deserved it so much, and seeing how she developed through the last year and how this jersey gave her wings was really inspiring.

You’ve had quite a tough year with a crash at La Vuelta. Is that the toughest thing you’ve had to come back from?

Yeah I think this injury was the biggest challenge I’ve had in my career yet. I broke my collarbone the year before, but my broken arm was definitely worse, and it took me quite a while to come back. But I’m really happy that I could come back strong.

In the moment it was really hard, and I doubted myself a lot – I couldn’t really find the answer why this had to happen. But I think in the end, these three months also taught me a lot, and I think I got out of it not physically stronger, but mentally a lot stronger. It’s a new experience that I have with me now, and I think it will help me in the upcoming years.

How did you get through those difficult months?

I was super-lucky. I could count on a very strong environment. My family were behind me since day one. My mum flew to the hospital in Spain, and then she came back with me to Switzerland. She was a really big help this whole time. But also, the whole staff of the team, the team doctors organised everything really well together with our doctors in Switzerland. The whole medical staff of Swiss Olympic worked super hard, and my national coach as well. So it was like one big family, everyone together, trying to help me get back on my bike as quick as possible, and I felt really supported.

So I never felt really alone in this situation. I always knew I had a whole group behind me that wants the best for me and really cares about me, and that gave me a calm mindset that it’s gonna be fine; the injury happened, and now it’s out of my control, and I can only control how I react to it. I wanted to do that with 100% commitment, just to use every day the best that I could to get back as quick as possible, depending on the day, doing what my body could do the best possible way. The time actually went really quick. I went to the physio a lot and tried to do some other things as well besides cycling. Just spend time with family and friends, and I think that helped the recovery process as well.

What else did you do to pass the time?

I was stressed or quite busy all the time. I was never really bored because in the first few days obviously everything takes more time, even to get dressed or to shower. So you’re busy with those things, and then I had to go to the physio every second day. I had appointments with the doctors. So time was actually passing really quick. I could already go back on the trainer one week after the surgery. In the beginning was only really short training, but then I had something to do. So actually I wasn’t really bored. I went to some ice hockey games, which I really enjoyed. Did a lot of baking and cooking in the kitchen, things like that.

Talk us through your journey into cycling.

I have an older brother, Timon. He’s five years older, and he’s a professional mountain biker. And my father used to be a cyclist as well when he was younger. So cycling was always a family thing. My brother started racing earlier than me, obviously, and we always went to watch his cyclocross races on the weekend as a family. At first I was really not interested, but then I had to change my school from primary to secondary, and I had to go by bike, and since that moment I totally fell in love with it – I felt the freedom and was like, “Yeah, I want to try this out as well.” I borrowed a bike from a friend and then I rode my first cyclocross race a few weeks after that. Then it became a family thing, every weekend was filled with cyclocross races and then a few years after, I started to race more on the road, and then made the switch.

We often think of Swiss riders as excellent time-triallists, but you have come to the sport from the off-road route. Did growing up in Switzerland influence your direction?

I did some mountain biking as well, [which] is also really big in Switzerland. But I soon realised that wasn’t for me, and actually by the time that I started on the road, we had Fabian Cancellara, but Marlen [Reusser] didn’t race at that time yet, so it was kind of difficult because there were no women I could look up to that were in the WorldTour – I had to find a bit my own way. I think now we actually built up a really strong women’s squad on the road, so that young girls can come after us and have something to look up to and a pathway that is already there for them. But at the time I started, it was a bit challenging to find my own way.

Who inspired you when you were getting into cycling?

Good question. I think by the time I started, it was for sure more male athletes, like Fabian Cancellara was big idol for me, but also because I did a lot of cyclocross, I was always a big fan of Wout van Aert. I still am now. Those were my idols, but also my brother. I always looked up to him, and he helped me a lot in this whole path because everything I had to go through, I knew he went through already, so I could always ask him for help or for his advice. And I always wanted to be as strong as him – that was one of my big motivations as well.

We know you as a really versatile rider. What’s your favourite kind of race to ride?

I really like it if it’s on from the beginning and a hard race with not a lot of rest. I like the punchy climbs, between two- and five-minute efforts, again and again, and then a reduced sprint at the end. For me, one of my favourite races for sure is Milan-San Remo. It’s a big goal for me to win this race one day. But also races like Flanders, where you have all these short but steep climbs, and it’s just a brutal race, or even a race like Liège. So yeah, I’m quite versatile, and I can make use of my really good power-to-weight ratio. I can get over the climbs, but I can also sprint at the end, and I think that’s my superpower.

What’s been your favourite memory in cycling so far?

Probably what I will always remember is the first edition of San Remo, where I finished on the podium in third place. That was just a really amazing experience because it was a big goal, but it was the first edition, so nobody knew how it would play out, and we didn’t know really what to expect. But we had such a great team plan, and everyone committed so well. And then that I was able to finish it off was really amazing. That was my first podium in a Monument.

Also my first WorldTour win in Australia when I won on Willunga Hill in the Tour Down Under, because this was a solo victory, and I think that’s one of the most beautiful wins you can have in cycling if you win solo. I think this was the start of my breakthrough that really gave me the confidence to know I can be up there and I belong with the best of the world, and ever since I was quite consistent in all of the races, actually. So, I would say one of those two.

You’ve won the Tour Down Under twice in a row now, what is it about Australia that works for you so well?

I really like Australia. I just love the atmosphere there. It’s so relaxed, and the people are super-nice. It almost feels a bit like a holiday to get there. But also I can really lock in and have a good training block at home, and I really love training at home. So the winter time is always this period where I’m home most, and I can really focus on training, but also I think I have a really good balance between training and mental recovery. In the winter I do a lot of other stuff. I can go out with friends, go to hockey games and stuff. I think that I always come out so strong because I can focus on training, but I also really enjoy life. And then I go to the race and I feel mentally totally recovered, but physically I’m in really good shape.

Also now after my injury, I had this block at home where I could train and do other things, and I came really strong out of it. So I think there is something for me, about the fact of spending time at home, because we travel so much during the year, sometimes you lose yourself a bit when you travel from one to the other race and training camp, and it just gets too much. And I think then you can’t produce the same performance in the race.

You’ve been at EF for a while now. Tell us what’s working for you there and why it’s such a good team to be a part of.

Yeah, I’m super-happy. I found my place at EF. I think it’s a super-good match for me. Comparing it to other teams, I would say it’s like the fans’ favourite team, I think we really show that cycling is not all about results, but also about having fun and inspiring others, having a great team culture. Everyone gets accepted as the rider they are and the personality behind, and you don’t feel like you need to fit into a certain box.

Of course, we want to have good results, but I think this is the first step. If you have fun and you feel good and happy in your place, and you enjoy the atmosphere, you have the right people around, then the results and the performance will come automatically. I think sometimes teams try to focus too much on results, and it gets so serious that you forget to actually enjoy and have fun, and then you won’t get great results either.

Women’s cycling is developing fast. What further improvements would you like to see to the women’s side of the sport?

Yeah, we’ve come a really long way, and over the past few years it developed super-quick. We probably can’t continue at that speed because I think teams need time to adjust to it. I think at the moment we are in a really good place, and it’s okay to realise, this is actually a good place, and we don’t always need to get more and more and better because I think we will never be really equal to the men. I think it’s not possible, and also it’s not needed.

It’s just about continuing like this and holding this standard, and of course it would be nice to get more sponsors into women’s cycling or get longer TV coverage, but in my opinion, we are already in a really good spot. Comparing it to other women’s sports, I think cycling is one of the most developed.

Finally, what brings you joy off the bike?

Ice hockey games. Just spending a lot of time with family and friends, cooking, baking. I enjoy really good coffee. Just being out in the nature, connecting to myself.

The post ‘I found my place at EF’: Noemi Rüegg Q&A appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Ari Cascade Peak Pro Review: Affordable and Adaptable – Travis Engel
entry.content:
Designing and speccing a budget full-suspension bike is a puzzle, and every brand solves it differently. They predict where a customer is willing to splurge, and where they want to save. Travis thinks the Ari Cascade Peak strikes an even balance, in more ways than one.

If you’re shopping for a high-end carbon full suspension bike, you’re spoiled for choice these days. Not only between brands, but within brands. Most offer four or five price points in each model. But there’s no such bounty on the alloy end of the spectrum. You’re lucky to get two builds: The cheap one that makes far too many compromises, and the one you should actually buy.

Ari Cascade Peak Pro Quick Hits

  • 135mm rear travel, 140mm front
  • 29” wheels, front and rear
  • Alloy frame only
  • Two in-triangle bottle cages on all sizes
  • 35.9 lbs (XL w/o pedals)
  • Assorted spec customizations available at purchase
  • Assembled in Utah
  • Sold consumer-direct
  • Entry-level build starts at $2,199
  • $3,384 as tested

The Ari Cascade Peak lineup is different. This 135mm rear-travel, 140mm front-travel do-it-all trail bike comes in three stock builds: The $2,200 Comp, the $2,800 Elite, and the $3,300 Pro. I usually save spec talk for the end of my reviews, but this one deserves a spotlight. I’d never been so torn on which price point to cover.

I leaned towards the Comp at first. It’s impressive to get in under $3K in 2026. Its DVO suspension has a boutique cache, with bonus versatility points for the fork’s 36mm stanchions. And it runs on the proven Deore 6100 drivetrain with a proper 10-51 12-speed Micro Spline cassette. But then the base-level Comp grabbed me. Its MicroShift AdventX drivetrain has a populist appeal, and its Shimano two-piston brakes are better than Tektro. Though  when speccing suspension, I think it was brave for Ari to go off-brand. At lower pricepoints, a Suntour fork and shock are often better than similarly priced RockShox stuff.

But I ultimately chose the Pro build. Deore 7200 may become the benchmark for affordable high-end hanger-mount cable-actuated drivetrains. And Ari swapped in an XT 8200 shifter for its double-upshift capability. The Reynolds alloy rims will save some unsprung rotational weight, and the recently updated TRP EVO Expert brake is remarkably powerful. The Marzocchi suspension is the Cascade Peak Pro’s most meaningful upgrade. Marzocchi is now the Fox budget label, with similar functionality, a little less adjustability, and a little more weight. There’s lots to say about it, but I’ll save that for the ride impressions.

Customization and Ordering

Ari assembles their bikes in their Utah headquarters. That makes for improved quality control, wider inventory flexibility, and a few more American jobs. It also allows for customizations and substitutions. Far more than other locally assembled brands like Pivot and Yeti offer. The Cascade Peak’s add-to-cart process includes tweaks like adding a tubeless setup, upgrading your wheels, or applying frame protection. But I got my build with 50mm rise bars and a 230mm dropper post, which were technically off-menu. If you want something that’s not in the drop-downs email Ari and they may be able to accommodate. Just email them. It’s a surprisingly concierge-level process. I even got texts as my review bike went through picking, building, checking, and shipping.

Of course, Ari is only able to offer that experience at these prices because they sell consumer-direct. Given that this review shares server space with The Radavist’s many shop visits and human stories, I need to acknowledge that high-end consumer-direct sales are a disruptive force among US retailers. I try to call that out when I review these bikes, but that doesn’t mean I get to have it both ways. In the grand scheme of things, I believe it’s good that consumer-direct bikes are an option. Especially budget-friendly ones like the Ari Cascade Peak.

Ari Cascade Peak Frame Design

The Cascade Peak is effectively the alloy version of the all-carbon Delano Peak, which has 10 mm more fork travel, and a longer-stroke shock for an extra 7 mm out back. Ari gave these two models unique names so they were free to evolve at different intervals, and potentially even in different directions. Thankfully, the Cascade Peak seems pretty future-proof. Its Horst-style linkage doesn’t really take any chances, nor should it. The pivots are all bearings, and they’re all big. There’s a flip chip (in its default “low” setting) that’s so sleek, I didn’t notice it until I was cleaning the bike ahead of its return. It’s got a threaded bottom bracket, press-in headset cups, ample tire clearance, and a pretty slick paint job.

I do have a few nitpicks. The cables rattled inside the frame, though Ari jiu-jitsu’d that into something praise-worthy. I brought it up in a debrief with Tyler Cloward, Ari’s Director of Product Development. A few days later, he said they took the note and will make a rolling change to foam-line their unguided internal housing at no extra charge.

Fair play, Ari. Now route your shift housing through the top of the chainstay not the bottom. It makes for a smoother line than the Cascade Peak’s under-stay exit, though I know it’s far from the only bike that does it. Another note while we’re back there: The chainstay protection is ample, but my foot began peeling it off on my very first ride. A few zip ties fixed it, but the stays are relatively wide if you know you’re particularly sensitive to heel clicking. And finally, the frame has an oddly tall silhouette. But there’s a very good reason for that.

This is the second bike in a row I’ve tested with two in-triangle bottle cages, and I hope it’s the next big trend in trail bikes. Especially given the hot summer we’ve had here in LA, I’ve been thankful to stay hydrated without the aid of a full-sized hydration pack. It’s a quantitative increase with qualitative impact. I can carry nearly 100 ounces of water by adding a two-bottle hip pack. Or I can just rely on my bib pockets, and still get 44 ounces. One bottle can be for water, the other can be for fancy chemicals. And there’s still a little pocket of space at the front of the triangle to strap on an essentials kit, though I wouldn’t have minded an accessory port. Of course, I could strap my essentials to the under-downtube mount. Or, I could run a third bottle.

Ari Cascade Peak Geometry

Depending on how you measure standover, all that storage comes at a cost of 20 to 30 mm of clearance compared to similar single-bottle bikes. But I think standover is more about form than function. A low top tube makes a mountain bike look like it came to party. And while the Cascade Peak is no pooper, it’s more about broad versatility than pure velocity. Its 65° head angle is conservative by today’s trail-bike standards, as is its wheelbase. The high-ish bottom bracket favors pedaling over plantedness, and the 434mm chainstays (across all sizes) are about as short as they come in this category. And yet, it’s got a burly fork, big rotors, and brakes that have become downhill darlings. If you’re looking for a bike that’ll clearly tell you what it wants, this isn’t it. So, what does it want?

Ari Cascade Peak Ride Impressions: Climbing

I reviewed Ari’s (then Fezz-ari’s) La Sal peak in 2018, and I gushed about its 78° seat-tube angle. It was revolutionary back then, and it’s actually still pretty steep today. It pairs well with the Cascade Peak’s active rear suspension. It’s got a slightly floaty feel that is saved from wallowing by its forward weight bias. But that means it isn’t the kind of mid-travel trail bike that encourages you to mash at race pace. The Pivot Trailcat and Ibis Ripley are much more energetic. The Cascade Peak favors plushness over pep. That means I relied on the lockout lever to optimize long, smooth climbs, which is a fair trade for how this bike performed when things got technical.

There wasn’t that magical hoverbike effect offered by some DW and CBF bikes that provides a stable platform while the rear wheel simultaneously pours effortlessly through obstacles. But the Cascade Peak would yield with impeccable consistency. There was no sudden drop-off or unwelcomed ramp-up in support. That offered a lot of freedom in setups. I tend to want a little deeper sag in my rear suspension, and there were no mushy consequences when I took poor lines or showed poor form. And I had to do both at the same time to get my foot in the dirt. After a month of testing, only one pedal strike was severe enough to remember.

Equally forgiving on the climbs was the Cascade Peak’s wheelbase. To be fair, I’ve spent a number of years riding enduro bikes as daily drivers. Your mileage may vary, but the Cascade Peak should be easy for anyone to get used to. In a word, its climbing vibe is “comfortable.” That suits a bike like this rather well. The ample on-bike storage was ideal for epic rides at steady paces. Meanwhile, its spec and chassis adeptly handled most of the descents I found along the way … but not all of them.

Ari Cascade Peak Ride Impressions: Descending

Bikes in this travel category often suffer from an identity crisis. They’re not as plush as all-mountain bikes, and they’re not as zippy as short-travel trail bikes. A brand can inject some personality with a high pivot and long chainstay like the Forbidden Druid or an extravagant lightweight build like the Pivot Trailcat LT. The Cascade Peak does neither, and yet it still makes some clear choices in its on-trail behavior. Namely; it likes the techy stuff.

Just like on the climbs, it’s quite agreeable to quick maneuvers on awkward terrain. That’s not true of many bikes north of 130mm rear travel. But the consistency I sensed on the climbs returned to help make the Cascade Peak remarkably responsive on the descents. It was easy to pop one or both wheels off the ground to maintain the right line with the right momentum. Paired with the moderate geo, this made for a nimble ride that I wouldn’t have expected from a bike with this much travel and this much mass.

If you like the sound of that, I do recommend opting for taller bars. I mean, I always recommend taller bars, but defaulting to a more upright, mid-bike body position gave me a better starting point when making these maneuvers. It also helped on straighter, faster descents. And the Cascade Peak does need a little help in that department.

I need to first acknowledge that my career in covering high-end mountain bikes has left me a little spoiled. That usually doesn’t get in the way when I’m reviewing affordable bikes like the Cascade Peak. My overall judgement is never clouded by the absence (or presence) of carbon wheels or electronic drivetrains. But suspension is different, especially front suspension. High-end dampers can combine support and sensitivity in ways simpler designs can’t. And the Marzocchi Z1’s Rail damper is indeed a simple design. It’s robust and low-maintenance, but it lacks the speed-sensitive nuances of Fox’s Grip damper or RockShox’s Charger.

On the trail, that meant high-intensity impacts were a little harsh off the top. To my surprise, though, the fork wasn’t diving excessively or getting otherwise overwhelmed. The ride height defaulted up where I wanted it. But at high speeds and on rough terrain, I couldn’t get into the flow a bike like this should be capable of. Again, keep in mind I’m coming off a Fox 36 SL, which itself followed the almost-too-plush RockShox Lyrik Linear XL. Those are extremely high bars. Once I had acclimated to the Z1’s feel, its relatively mild shortcomings became less and less distracting. And to many Cascade Peak customers, it may be the best fork they’ve ever ridden.

The 36mm chassis is a smart long-term choice for a versatile bike that may end up literally anywhere. But as an experiment on my last few rides, I swapped it for a Fox fork equipped with their Grip X damper. It made a significant difference. The whole bike was suddenly able to float more calmly through chunder.

This got me thinking about Ari’s customization. Cloward tells me they technically could accommodate a buyer’s request to upgrade to a higher-end fork. But that would bump the highest-end Cascade Peak Pro up to within a few hundred bucks of the $4,200 entry-level Delano Peak Comp. That bike’s DVO Diamond 36 D1 SL offers speed-sensitive damping tech similar to what makes Fox’s 36 Grip X damper so ubiquitous in the high end. And it’s got a carbon frame. Or there’s the $5,300 Delano Peak Expert, which gets a highly tunable 36 Grip X2 damper, plus upgrades nearly everywhere else.

But let’s take a step back from that slippery slope. If I’ve made you doubt the Cascade Peak’s front suspension performance, but the bike is already at the top of your price range, you can always upgrade the fork damper to a Grip X. You can easily make the swap at home with a chamferless socket bit. And it’s $320, which is about half what it’d cost for Ari to upgrade to a Fox 36. You’ll still have a more basic air spring, but so did the two-generation-old Fox fork I bolted on. And anyway, I said no more slippery slopes. You can make this upgrade at any point down the road. There’s no rush. But if that time comes, the bike deserves it.

The rest of the build lives up to the bike’s potential. That Deore 7200 drivetrain shifts great and is surprisingly quiet despite its clutch-less-ness. It seemed somehow calmer than my XTR Di2 drivetrain. Maybe because it gets support from a length of stiff SIS housing, and because it lacks the weight of a motor and battery. The recently updated TRP brakes are just as impressive. The sharp bend at the blade tip is a bit love-or-hate, but the power is all love. They feel a lot like Hayes Dominion A4, if you’ve ever been fortunate enough to try those.

The TranzX dropper post is fast and firm, the Continental Xynotal / Kryptotal tires are overkill in the best way, and … well, look at that. I am ending on spec. I guess it’s an important factor here. If we were talking about a $6,500 mountain bike, we could rightly assume it would offer total functional perfection. It’s not so simple at half the price, but the Cascade Peak Pro manages with very few compromises.

All that’s left is to explain what kind of mountain bike it is. To outline its likes and dislikes. Again, the Cascade Peak likes little techy sections and big long pedals. But it’s well enough equipped that it has very few dislikes. That’s how it should be in this broadly appealing category at this broadly appealing price point. It’ll handle just about any trail you put in front of it without ever leaving you wishing it was anything other than exactly what it is.

Pros:

  • Surprisingly nimble for a mid-travel trail bike
  • Comfortable climbing position
  • Two in-triangle bottle cages!
  • Worth upgrading down the road
  • Good value
  • Smart spec
  • Wide customization options

Cons:

  • Fork is a bit harsh at high speeds
  • Geometry isn’t as DH-ready as that of some bikes in this travel category

See more at Ari

The post Ari Cascade Peak Pro Review: Affordable and Adaptable appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: ‘I’ve been good in 2026, but I prefer to be outstanding at least one or two days a year’: Michael Storer Q&A
entry.content:
Cyclist
‘I’ve been good in 2026, but I prefer to be outstanding at least one or two days a year’: Michael Storer Q&A

Can you remember the first bike race you won and how?

Not the very first, but one of the first was this really hilly club race in a town called Brigadoon in Australia. I was 12 and it was probably one of the hardest loops you could make in Perth, with these steep ramps with 20% gradients up and downhill. It was maybe only 30 or 40km long, but it was a pure climber’s course and I won it solo. I did appreciate the $30 bike voucher that they gave us as a prize in those days too. You could get quite a lot with that: a couple of spare tubes, a new bike light or maybe some other accessories.

There are a number of pro cyclists who come from Perth; there’s you, Jai Hindley, Ben O’Connor…

Luke Durbridge, Cam Meyer…

What’s in the water? What has made it such a hotspot for cyclists?

It was mostly thanks to Jai’s dad [Gordon]. He was just one of the coaches there who influenced Midland Cycle Club and pushed it in a direction that was better for high performance. He had some contagious enthusiasm, he was really good at getting a lot more kids involved and he knew a thing or two about pro cycling as well. That made a big difference to the club’s general culture.

You were studying a chemistry degree at university and considering doing that over pro cycling. What changed your mind?

It was more splitting the approach, not putting all my eggs in one basket. I still had some belief in pro cycling, of course, but I was keeping the studying alive just in case. I also switched to psychology for the last year, but I stopped studying when I signed my pro contract [in 2017] – until then, you never know. If you really want to maximise being a pro cyclist, I think it’s almost better if you don’t study. It comes with risk of burnout as well.

While your breakthrough came at the 2021 Vuelta with two stage wins, it seems like joining Tudor Pro Cycling in 2024 coincided with a rise in your consistency and performance. What changed?

After what was kind of two lost years at Groupama-FDJ [in 2022 and 2023], I was restarting where I left off. I still won the Tour de l’Ain [in 2023], so it wasn’t all bad, but I didn’t progress that extra bit. Groupama didn’t have the support to bring me to a higher level. At Tudor I have that support to find that extra bit of improvement, which can really make a difference in results.

They just work on everything. It can be something as basic as bike positioning, both on the time-trial and road bike, which is super-important. There’s better coaching, and the team culture has a big influence. I feel a lot more motivated to do well in this team and it makes a difference if you feel good, then you have more of a positive mindset to impact your form. At previous teams it maybe wasn’t the best environment and I’d be looking forward to going home each time after a race.

You’re more of a climber than anything else. Do you think climbers have a different personality type to sprinters?

With the nature of sprinting, you have to be a bit more assertive, borderline aggressive; in climbing, you don’t necessarily need those characteristics to be successful.

You’ve lived mainly in Italy and San Marino since 2016. Have you picked up any Italian traits?

Probably being critical over food; no cappuccino past 12 o’clock; no undercooked or over-cooked pasta. Also, I hate it if the sauce is undercooked and watery.

What are your thoughts about pineapple on pizza?

Definitely not.

Your diet is plant-based. Have you noticed gains in terms of performance or feeling?

That’s the right way to describe it – plant-based, not plant-exclusive – I’ve had one steak this year because I like it once a year, a little treat at a training camp. The main benefit initially was just better knowledge of nutrition. I haven’t done a PubMed [database of health articles] search and there isn’t much research on vegan diet and performance yet the consensus is there’s no impact, which is good. If there’s no negatives and positive other things, then why not?

You finished third at Il Lombardia in 2025 to Tadej Pogačar. What was that experience like, going toe-to-toe with the dominant force in cycling?

Surreal. I was confident of a top ten, which was the goal, and I remember feeling good on the second-to-last climb. I was counting the number of guys left in the group, which also gives motivation. Then I heard on the radio about some strong riders getting dropped, including Del Toro and Seixas. So at least if he [Seixas] is the next Pogačar, I can say I beat him once.

That day I went super-deep. I could hardly stand up at the finish line. I could feel muscle failure, it hurt just walking up and down the podium steps; proper pain. That’s when you know you’ve gone extremely deep.

Did Pogačar at least look drained?

No, the usual jumping around, smiling – I was smiling too, but couldn’t jump anymore. He said, ‘Well done.’ I think he was a little bit surprised to see me on the podium.

Has that helped your confidence?

Even if it happens once a season, if I have that one day where I’m flying and get a top result, that’s super-exciting. I hope to get the ball rolling a bit more. I’ve been thereabouts in 2026, I’ve been good, but I prefer to be outstanding at least one or two days a year.

The post ‘I’ve been good in 2026, but I prefer to be outstanding at least one or two days a year’: Michael Storer Q&A appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: UCI World Championships 2026 Men’s Elite Road Race: Our form guide
entry.content:
Cyclist
UCI World Championships 2026 Men’s Elite Road Race: Our form guide

Prepare yourself for one of the most wide open rainbow jersey fights in a long time. Defending champion Tadej Pogačar is out following his crash at the Vuelta a España, and plenty of riders will be relishing the opportunity to fight for the jersey in the men’s elite road race at the 2026 UCI World Championships.

Taking place in Montréal, Canada on Sunday 27th September, the 273.7km course begins in Brossard and eventually gets to a hilly 13.4km circuit around Mount Royal Park, which includes Voie Camillien-Houde (1.7km, 7.7%) and Côte de Polytechnique (0.8km, 5.7%). The riders will complete 12 laps to total 3,803m of elevation by the end, which is 200m more than the GP Montréal race, won this year by Isaac del Toro, which uses the same circuit but over a shorter 214.4km distance.

Isaac del Toro (Mexico)

He’s only 22 years old, but Mexico’s Isaac del Toro is the favourite here, cementing his status after winning the GP Montréal. Pogačar’s teammate and protégé, Del Toro will be relishing the opportunity to ride for himself here, especially without Pogačar to compete with. Having become the first Mexican to finish on the podium of the Tour de France in 2026, he could be the first to win here too.

He added a whole host of victories to his growing palmarès this year, including overall stage race wins at the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico and Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. Unless something goes badly wrong, he will undoubtably improve on his seventh place on his elite race debut last year, the only question is: what colour will his medal be?

Road victories this season

  • Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal 
  • GC: Lidl Deutschland Tour
  • Prologue: Lidl Deutschland Tour
  • Stage 2: Tour de France
  • GC: Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes
  • Stage 8: Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes
  • Stage 7: Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes
  • GC: Tirreno-Adriatico
  • Stage 6: Tirreno-Adriatico
  • GC: UAE Tour
  • Stage 6: UAE Tour
  • Stage 1: UAE Tour

Last five results

  • 6th: World Championship Elite Men Individual Time-Trial
  • 1st: Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal 
  • 55th: Grand Prix Cyclist de Quebec
  • 1st overall: Lidl Deutschland Tour
  • 17th: Lidl Deutschland Tour, Stage 4

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 7th: 2025

Paul Seixas (France)

The young riders are generating all the buzz this year. Like Del Toro, Frenchman Paul Seixas is having a meteoric rise, riding to fourth overall at the Tour on his debut this year. He was frequently best of the rest behind Pogačar in the hilly Classics in the spring, notching second places at Strade Bianche and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and also won La Flèche Wallonne with its nasty kick uphill in the Muy de Huy to finish. He finished second behind Del Toro at the GP Montréal having been a solo leader before the Mexican caught him and beat him to the line.

Seixas bypassed the U23 rankings to finish 13th in the elite race on his first attempt last year having previously won an ITT gold medal in the junior Worlds in 2024.

Road victories this season

  • La Flèche Wallonne
  • GC: Itzulia Basque Country
  • Stage 5: Itzulia Basque Country
  • Stage 2: Itzulia Basque Country
  • Stage 1 ITT: Itzulia Basque Country
  • Faun-Ardèche Classic 
  • Stage 2: Volta ao Algarve

Last five results

  • 3rd: World Championship Elite Men Individual Time-Trial
  • 2nd: Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal 
  • 17th: Grand Prix Cyclist de Quebec
  • 4th overall: Tour de France
  • 47th: Stage 21, Tour de France

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 13th: 2025

Remco Evenepoel (Belgium)

Is the double on the cards? Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel just blitzed the field to claim his fourth consecutive elite individual time-trial gold medal and has won three of his last four races entered in the Donostia San Sebastian Klasikoa, Grand Prix Cyclist de Quebec and the Worlds ITT. This one-day form should serve him well as he hunts his first road race rainbows since 2022, and the first ever elite road and TT double. If anyone can do it it’s the double Olympic champion.

Road victories this season

  • World Championship Elite Men Individual Time-Trial
  • Grand Prix Cyclist de Quebec
  • Donostia San Sebastian Klasikoa
  • Stage 16 ITT: Tour de France
  • Stage 15: Tour de France
  • Amstel Gold Race
  • Stage 2 ITT: UAE Tour
  • GC: Volta Comunitat Valenciana
  • Stage 4: Volta Comunitat Valenciana
  • Stage 2 ITT: Volta Comunitat Valenciana
  • Trofeo Andratx-Pollença
  • Trofeo Serra Tramuntana
  • Trofeo Ses Salines

Last five results

  • 1st: World Championship Elite Men Individual Time-Trial
  • 5th: Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal 
  • 1st: Grand Prix Cycliste de Quebec
  • 1st: Donostia San Sebastian Klasikoa
  • 2nd overall: Tour de France

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 1st: 2022

Mathieu van der Poel (Netherlands)

Mathieu van der Poel is in scintillating form, having just pulled off a successful 174km solo breakaway to win the final day at the Tour de Luxembourg. This summer he also won two stages at the Tour de France including the scintillating final stage in Paris.

The Classics extraordinaire raced to victory at Omloop Nieuwsblad and the E3 Saxo Classic this season but came second to Pogačar at the Tour of Flanders and finished just off the podium in Paris-Roubaix after a series of unfortunate mechanicals in the Arenberg forest. Van der Poel won road Worlds in Glasgow in 2023, but he should really be one to take advantage of a Pogačar-less race with this kind of parcours.

Road victories this season

  • Stage 5: Tour de Luxembourg
  • Stage 1: Tour de Luxembourg
  • Stage 21: Tour de France
  • Stage 9: Tour de France
  • E3 Saxo Classic
  • Stage 4: Tirreno-Adriatico
  • Stage 2: Tirreno-Adriatico
  • Omloop Nieuwsblad

Last five results

  • 19th overall: Tour de Luxembourg
  • 1st: Stage 5, Tour de Luxembourg
  • 61st: Stage 4 ITT, Tour de Luxembourg
  • 52nd: Stage 3, Tour de Luxembourg
  • 5th: Stage 2, Tour de Luxembourg

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 1st: 2023

Tom Pidcock (Great Britain)

Freshly crowned MTB XCO World Champion Tom Pidcock is in great form, winning the GP Industria & Artigianato, finishing just off the podium at the GP Quebec and sixth at GP de Montréal in his first road races after MTB Worlds. Pidcock is a true one-day talent, despite his GC form over the past few years, and with cyclocross and MTB world titles to his name, this is the best opportunity he’ll get to add road to his set.

While he has a junior time-trial gold medal and bronze in the U23 road race to boast about, his best placing in the elite race came back in 2021 with sixth place.

Road victories this season

  • GP Industria & Artigianato
  • Andorra MoraBanc Clàssica
  • Stage 3: Tour of the Alps
  • Milano-Torino
  • Stage 5: Vuelta a Andalucia

Last five results

  • 6th: Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal 
  • 4th: Grand Prix Cycliste de Quebec
  • 1st: GP Industria & Artigianato
  • 9th overall: Tour de France
  • 125th: Stage 21, Tour de France

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 6th: (2021)

Wout van Aert (Belgium)

This has been a great year for Wout van Aert. The Belgian finally won Paris-Roubaix, and took stages at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and Tour of Denmark before a phenomenal Vuelta a España campaign that resulted in two wins for him and the points classification, plus five wins for teammate Matthew Brennan.

He has twice finished second in the World Championships road race. First to Julian Alaphilippe in 2020 and then to Van der Poel in 2023. A rainbow jersey would make this quite the season for Van Aert, though with Evenepoel on his team he won’t have a full squad of helpers – though having two cards to play may help.

Road victories this season

  • Stage 15: Vuelta a España
  • Stage 13: Vuelta a España
  • Overall: Tour of Denmark
  • Stage 3: Tour of Denmark
  • Stage 2: Tour of Denmark
  • Stage 1: Tour of Denmark
  • Stage 5: Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes
  • Stage 3 TTT: Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes
  • Paris-Roubaix

Last five results

  • 44th overall: Vuelta a España
  • 65th: Stage 21, Vuelta a España
  • 30th: Stage 20, Vuelta a España
  • 97th: Stage 19, Vuelta a España
  • 5th: Stage 18 ITT, Vuelta a España

Best finish in World Championship Elite Road Race

  • 2nd: 2020, 2023

Other contenders

This feels a very different rainbow jersey fight given the absence of Pogačar. It could well give us a surprise winner.

Ben Healy (Ireland) raced to a bronze medal last year and has a tenacity for a long, hard day in the saddle where he can go solo. Mauro Schmid (Switzerland) scored high placings in the Classics this year and won a stage at the Tour too, similarly if a move of outsiders gets clear he could certainly win. Quinn Simmons (United States) has had a fantastic season, with standout performances at the Tour de France, and more recently ninth at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic, fifth at the GP Quebec and fourth at the GP de Montréal, he’ll certainly be acclimatised to the time zone.

There’s also Juan Ayuso (Spain), Tobias Halland Johannessen (Norway), Christian Scaroni, Giulio Ciccone and Giulio Pellizzari (Italy), plus Florian Lipowitz (Germany) to keep an eye on. And it could be none of them – international racing often brings chaos.

The post UCI World Championships 2026 Men’s Elite Road Race: Our form guide appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Ride with GPS Launches 3D Maps
entry.content:
Ride with GPS recently announced the addition of 3D Maps, now live on the web and in the mobile app…

Flat maps have always forced riders to imagine the parts that matter most: the massive switchbacking climb and the ridge that drops into the valley. A contour line or a patch of terrain shading only goes so far. 3D Maps fundamentally changes that, letting riders tilt, rotate, and zoom into any route to visualize the terrain the way they’ll actually experience it.

3D Maps

3D Maps isn’t just a cosmetic upgrade. It completely transforms the way riders prepare for and experience routes, ultimately leading to better rides. The feature is built around three ways riders already use the map:

  • Preview in 3D — see the shape of a climb or descent before committing to a route, then tack on other tools like Community Photos, Heatmaps, and Advanced Layers to get a complete read on what to expect.
  • Plan in 3D — visually spot the tough sections right away and build a route to incorporate some extra climbing (or to avoid it entirely); regardless, planning in 3D makes the process much more fun and engaging.
  • Navigate in 3D — get real terrain context while riding, on a commute across town or a tour across the mountains, all while getting turn-by-turn directions to guide the way.

Riders aren’t locked into one look, either. 3D Maps work across Ride with GPS Cycle, OSM-based maps, ESRI Topo, and USGS-based styles, with satellite imagery available on mobile for even more terrain detail.

Different map styles offer unique information that can be critical to the route planning process for a specific area or style of riding. For a lot of riders, being able to analyze terrain using their preferred map style, as well as switching between others, gives them complete confidence in what to expect for the ride ahead.

3D Maps is live today on the web and in the Ride with GPS mobile app.

The post Ride with GPS Launches 3D Maps appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar Hands-On: AMOLED meets Solar?!?
entry.content:
Amazfit took one for the team. That’s probably the best way to describe the new Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar, which features a combined AMOLED display with not just one solar panel, but two entirely different solar panel systems. Since the first AMOLED displays came out years ago, people have been asking for companies (well, asking for Garmin, I suppose) to make a Fenix AMOLED Solar combo-dish.

But Garmin has long resisted that idea, stating simply that the power equation just didn’t make sense, and that it was better to take that extra space and simply stick a bigger battery in there. Still, many fans really, really, really wanted an AMOLED watch with solar panels nonetheless, doubting Garmin’s team of battery and solar engineers.

To which Amazfit said: Hold my beer. Actually, two beers.

And thus, here we are, with probably one of the geekiest watches of 2026, including both a front and rear solar panel (yes, on the back). And yes, we finally got an AMOLED-Solar hookup, rejoice!

Let’s dive into it, as I suspect it might be the only one we’ll ever see. Still, I’m all here for the geeky!

Some Quick Spec Differences:

Now, the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar is essentially a T-Rex Ultra 2 watch from a features standpoint, though there are some notable hardware differences. Still, Amazfit says it’s basically a twin to that watch.

Key Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar vs the Amazfit T-Rex Ultra 2 differences:

– Has a smaller 660mAh battery vs 870mAh on Ultra 2
– Has a smaller 1.3” AMOLED display vs 1.5” AMOLED display on Ultra 2
– Has deeper depth gauge allowance (50m, vs 45m on Ultra 2)
– Waterproofing spec of case is still 100m
– Has a white/red LED flashlight, vs white/green LED flashlight on Ultra 2
– Gains new LiveShare feature, though all Amazfit watches will gain this via App
– $649/649EUR ($100 more than Ultra 2 at $549/549EUR)

And then, from an overall standpoint, here’s how the Amazfit models differ – including notably the battery claims:

And then here’s a much deeper chart of battery details on the solar model:

At this point, it’s probably worthwhile noting that Amazfit says they aren’t trying to compete here with a MIP-based Fenix MIP/Solar model. Instead, they say that most people want that AMOLED screen, but the idea here is to offer that option to provide some extra battery gains via solar, if required.

The Solar Panel Features:

Now, I want to point out up front that while it’s clear the overall solar-to-gain equation here simply doesn’t work for any real-world scenario, what Amazfit has done around the user interface of the solar gains is so much better and more detailed than Garmin’s watch-based solar units. So, if there’s anything to take away from this watch, it’s probably that.

Still, we have to take a moment to appreciate what Amazfit has put together here, as I’m not aware of any other watch on the market with both front and rear solar panels. So, let’s start there, on the back of the watch.

This panel is obviously normally against your wrist, but the idea is that you can take the watch off your wrist during a break in a long adventure (such as a lunch break, or after you’ve hiked many hours and are done for the day), and then face it towards the sun. At which point, you’re gathering double the solar gains as the front panel. Amazfit says that the solar area is pretty close to double that of the front area, and equally, the gains are 2x that of the front panel.

There are a few things you’ll notice as a result of this. First, they’ve shifted the charging connector to the side of the watch, and gone with a different connector than all their other current-gen watches. This is a little bit of a bummer if you have something like their Amazfit Helio band for sleep instead (since now you need two different charging connectors), but I wouldn’t say it’s a deal breaker.

Next, is that with this rear-facing design, there’s a new ‘Solar Boost’ mode that gets activated when the rear-facing panel starts getting sun. You can technically also manually enable it, but practically speaking, once this thing ‘sees the light’, it pretty much activates immediately. That Solar Boost mode makes the rest of the watch inaccessible until you exit it.

Now, the main downside here is simply that the watch overheats in this flipped over mode really darn quick. Like, within 10 minutes quick in the toaster temperatures I live in (80-90°F/27-32°C). And once it does that, it doesn’t make any solar gains at all. Amazfit says in cooler temperatures (such as the top of a mountain), it’ll likely keep from overheating but still get plenty of solar juice.

Still, if you do the math here, even if I have to switch to the front panel, just 21 minutes of that is better than 10 minutes of the back panel, which then shuts off until it cools down. Nonetheless, that back panel, and the curvature into the optical HR sensor is super pretty/stunnng:

And certainly, in temperatures cooler than mine, it sounds like you won’t get overheating at all (such as in cooler alpine mountain temps).

When it comes to seeing those product gains, there’s a dedicated Solar widget. This widget starts off with a glance within the widget roll. From there, upon opening, you’ll see the last 4-hour graph, and the current/instant inbound power. Again, this is *NOT* total gains for the 4-hour duration, but rather the exact to-the-second current solar gains coming in:

However, that chart actually shows more than you might realize. It actually has two colors on it, such as below, showing both front panel and rear panel solar gains separately. I like this. Below you can see this where it was a bit breezier in the afternoon, and I managed to keep it cool enough:

In any case, below that you’ve got the Solar Index, which looks at the quality of the solar gains coming in. Again, you’ll notice the color coding.

And then finally, within this widget, there are gains materialized in the three core modes: Regular smartwatch mode, battery saver mode, and the watch-only mode (just time basically). I *really* like this, as it’s something that Garmin doesn’t do on their watches. Not so much the different modes, but they don’t show the battery gains (in days).

Note, however, this doesn’t account for your battery ‘losses’. Meaning, if you ‘lost’ 4 days of battery just by using the watch but gained 2 days from solar, you’re still at a 2-day loss. Also note, along the top you can change the timeframe 1d/7d/30d, which again, I rather like.

And all of this is also visible on the companion app too:

Next, back on the watch itself, there are a few final things I want to mention. First is that when you flip over the watch, it’ll automatically engage the rear panel. But, you can manually control that in the settings:

Likewise, you can manually force it into Solar Boost mode from the settings:

In the same place that you can force Battery Saver mode, as with any other Amazfit watch.

Now, for lack of anywhere else to mention it, the watch can indeed charge from completely dead (0%) using purely solar. So if you manage to kill it off, and then have a bunch of time to sit in the sun, it can jump-start it and get you back and cooking.

Ok, with that, let’s talk about some workouts, as well as general results from non-workout activity.

Real World Workouts and Gains:

I feel like every section here kinda has to start out with a ‘even if this boat sinks, at least they went down trying’. And in that case, I appreciate that Amazfit is pretty honest with the minimal gains you’d expect to see here in real-life conditions. In many ways, the solar aspects of this watch are really only useful if you’re in a situation where you’ve got pure blue-sky sun all day, but not using much of the watch itself beyond basic time operations.

Day out in sun with mostly back gains (roughly 6 hours):

Start day battery: 53% (9:45AM)
End day battery: 55% (3:15PM)
Note: Numerous overheat messages, don’t have battery % photos after 3PM, so just left gains above from 9-3PM

Another day out in the sun with mostly back gains (roughly 12 hours on back). I didn’t take a photo in the morning, but did take an evening photo with the solar gains listed:

Total time gained: 2.8d Smartwatch time
Total time gained: 8.4d Battery saver time
Total time gained: 14.0d Watch time
Note: Numerous overheat messages

And in fact, looking at each day I left it outside, it was almost always 2.5-3.0-days in smartwatch time gains via solar, regardless of whether it was front or back. That’s because on the back, it’d basically overheat (oscillating back and forth), whereas on the front it didn’t overheat (only once, I think), but gained less solar power (half the amount, but did it for consistently longer). But at the same time, it was also losing that amount each day in battery life, so it kinda ended up roughly a wash if I didn’t wear it at all (which defeats the point of the watch).

Next, a few different workouts. For fun, let’s actually start in the dark for an hour at night on a bike alongside my wife, who was doing a run for about 80 minutes. In this case, we can baseline the power draw (not always-on display, gesture-based, default GPS mode), with no solar gains:

Start battery: 45%
Duration: 1hr 20 mins
End battery: 42%
Loss per hour: ~2%
Note: At night, GPS enabled, no always-on display (gesture-based)

Next, we’ve got a 1-hour run yesterday. In this case, there were some initial scattered thin clouds, and I was getting about 30-40lux through that; then that single thin cloud moved on, and I was around 70-80lux. Obviously, occasional trees or body blockage, though I had tried to structure the route so that my wrist was mostly facing the sun.

Start battery: 43%
Duration: 1hr
End day battery: 41%
Loss per hour: 2%
Note: No overheat messages, generally quite sunny conditions, GPS enabled, no always-on display

Next, I went out for a 2-hour ride on a blue-sky sunny day. I even structured the route so that I had the watch facing the sun as much as possible for the ‘slower’ portions (gravel/ascending), and then more mixed for some of the faster descents.

However, for reasons that aren’t clear, it looks like the solar panel entirely failed to charge here. You can see that when I returned, the exact times the workout was going on, it showed zero solar power:

Amazfit is digging into it. There’s some theory that perhaps the automatic solar panel selection algorithm failed here and was actually activating the rear panel (they can’t operate concurrently), which would have been against my wrist. Still, even the moment the ride was saved/ended, solar charging resumed normally. Either way, here are those numbers:

Start battery: 51%
Duration: 2 hrs 12 mins
End battery: 46%
Loss per hour: ~2%
Note: No overheat messages, but also, seemingly no solar gains

Finally, here’s another nearly 3-hour ride, with mixed coverage. In this case, it was blue-sky sunny out, but some of the route and stoppage time had tree coverage, which reduced solar gains. But again, such is the real world:

Start battery: 16%
Duration: 2 hrs 57 mins
End battery: 10%
Loss per hour: ~2%
Note: No overheat messages, mixed sun conditions (due to trees)

Anyways, I’ll likely add in some more workouts with more data, though I think at this point there’s enough detail to get a relatively clear picture of battery gains from solar across various scenarios. Obviously, if you have less sun than I do, you’ll get less battery gains. Equally, if you have colder weather that’s still as sunny, you might get more gains from off-wrist scenarios.

Wrap-Up:

As I alluded to at the beginning, the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar is in many ways the very definition of form over function. But that’s OK. It delivered on the oft-asked request to merge together an AMOLED screen with solar, gains and battery life be damned.

And look – I appreciate Amazfit’s willingness to try and make this work. I think the back solar panel, and how it blends into the base of the optical heart rate sensor bump, looks great. Admittedly, I’ll almost never see it on my wrist, but hey, that’s kinda like having fancy underwear. Likewise, I really like Amazfit’s way of showing the battery gains in the solar widget. Though, I do wish they showed total cumulative lux hours throughout the day, similar to Garmin. But otherwise, the solar gains widget is just way more data practical/useful on Amazfit than Garmin.

Still, we can’t overlook the obvious here: The solar gains are, even in a best-case, crazy-sunny, stick-your-watch-outside-all-day scenario…basically negligible. In the days I stuck it outside all day, I gained a mere 2-3% of battery life. But equally, remember on those days I wasn’t wearing the watch (which would have consumed far more power with the display turning on optical HR sensors, algorithms, etc…). Once you put it on your wrist, as I showed during a GPS workout with body vs sun position/trees/etc… you quickly get to a near wash in battery gains between a sunny day and a night activity.

In other words, the reason AMOLED+SOLAR was resisted historically is because it simply didn’t make sense. You had to shrink your battery considerably in order to fit all the extra solar pieces in there (just like Amazfit did). And then you have to shrink your display to fit the solar ring around that (which Amazfit did). And then once you did those things, with the power draw of AMOLED, you were left with a watch that actually gets less battery life than what you started with (which is where Amazfit lands now). And that ignores that it’s also more expensive.

Nonetheless, as I said, first attempts don’t always work out. But hopefully Amazfit takes another swing at this down the road. I certainly don’t expect Amazfit to venture into MIP-based displays, especially as that market further dwindles. But I do like seeing a company push the bounds of things, even if it’s not quite a product I would buy.

With that, thanks for reading!

Found This Post Useful? Support The Site!

Hopefully you found this review/post useful. At the end of the day, I’m an athlete just like you looking for the most detail possible on a new purchase – so my review is written from the standpoint of how I used the device. The reviews generally take a lot of hours to put together, so it’s a fair bit of work (and labor of love). As you probably noticed by looking below, I also take time to answer all the questions posted in the comments – and there’s quite a bit of detail in there as well.

If you're shopping for the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar or any other accessory items, please consider using the affiliate links below! As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. It doesn’t cost you anything extra, but your purchases help support this website a lot.
